units.title: Hangul 1: vowels ㅏㅓㅗㅜㅡㅣ, consonants ㄱㄴㄷㄹ, hello

lessons.title: 1. The Korean alphabet
lessons.subtitle: Hangul · who made it and why · vowels and consonants

explanations.title: Hangul
explanations.body:
Koreans use their own unique alphabet, called Hangul. It was invented by King Sejong during the Chosun Dynasty (the book dates the dynasty 1393–1910) and was known as Hun-Min-Jeong-Eum, which literally means “the correct sounds for the instruction of the people”.

Before Hangul, Koreans used Chinese characters to write. The complicated characters were hard for ordinary people to read and write properly, so ordinary people were frustrated at not being able to put their thoughts and feelings into written words. King Sejong, a revolutionary ruler and scholar, imagined a set of uniquely Korean letters that would be easy to learn, and so Hun-Min-Jeong-Eum was born.

A note on spelling: the main English dictionary spelling is “Hangul”, but following the Revised Romanization of Korean the South Korean government writes “Hangeul” in its English publications. These lessons use “Hangul”. (The book’s video about Hangul is not included.)

explanations.title: How the letters were invented: the vowels
explanations.body: Every vowel was built from one of three symbols: a dot (•) for the heavens, a horizontal stick (ㅡ) for the earth, and a vertical stick (ㅣ) for a standing person. In writing, the dot became a short stroke attached to the long stick. Look at the short strokes below.

explanations.title: How the letters were invented: the consonants
explanations.body:
The consonants copy the position and shape of the mouth, tongue and lips as the sound is made. ㄱ, which sounds like the k in kimchi or the k at the end of book, shows the side view of the tongue as you say it: freeze your tongue the moment you say “k” and its shape looks like ㄱ.

Add a strong puff of air to ㄱ and you get ㅋ. The extra stroke in ㅋ stands for that puff of air.

ㄴ, which sounds like the n in now or ban, also shows the shape of the tongue as it is said. The book also shows drawings of the lips and tongue for ㅁ, ㅅ and ㅇ; those pictures are not reproduced here.

explanations.title: 21 vowels and 19 consonants
explanations.body:
Korean writing has 21 vowels and 19 consonants. For now, just get used to the shapes; you will meet each group in the next lessons.

A diphthong is two vowel sounds joined in one gliding movement. English examples are “ye” in yes, “ya” in yarn and “ea” in steak.

ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ and ㅉ are called double consonants, glottal consonants or tensed consonants.

exercises.prompt: In the design of the vowels, what does the dot stand for?
exercises.explanation: The dot stands for the heavens, the horizontal stick for the earth, the vertical stick for a standing person.

exercises.prompt: What does the extra stroke in ㅋ stand for?
exercises.explanation: Adding a strong puff of air to ㄱ gives ㅋ, and the extra stroke stands for the puff.

exercises.prompt: How many vowels and consonants are there in Hangul?
exercises.explanation: Korean writing has 21 vowels and 19 consonants.

exercises.prompt: Which group does ㅐ belong to?

exercises.explanation: ㅑ, ㅕ, ㅛ, ㅠ, ㅒ and ㅖ are the “Y” vowels.

exercises.explanation: ㅘ, ㅙ, ㅚ, ㅝ, ㅞ and ㅟ are the “W” vowels, which are diphthongs.

exercises.prompt: Which group does ㅌ belong to?
exercises.explanation: ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ and ㅊ are the aspirated consonants.

exercises.prompt: Which group does ㅆ belong to?
exercises.explanation: ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ and ㅉ are the double (glottal, tensed) consonants.

exercises.prompt: Which letter is the only one in the group of “other” vowels?
exercises.explanation: ㅢ is the one vowel that sits in the group of other vowels.

options: A consonant with a puff of air
Two vowel sounds joined in one gliding movement
exercises.explanation: A diphthong glides from one vowel sound to another, like “ye” in yes.

lessons.title: 2. Syllable blocks
lessons.subtitle: (C)V(C) · vertical and horizontal sticks · the placeholder ㅇ

explanations.title: A syllable is a block
explanations.body:
Syllables are the building blocks of words. The word kimchi has two syllables: kim and chi. In Korean a syllable has one optional initial consonant, a vowel, and one optional final consonant: (C)V(C). That gives four shapes of spoken syllable:

1. V: a vowel
2. CV: a consonant and a vowel
3. VC: a vowel and a consonant
4. CVC: a consonant, a vowel and a consonant

In writing, every syllable is fitted into an imaginary square block, for looks and for the sake of calligraphy.

explanations.title: Where the letters go in the block
explanations.body:
The initial consonant goes to the left of a vertical-stick vowel (ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅣ), or on top of a horizontal-stick vowel (ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ). In 가 the ㄱ stands to the left of ㅏ because ㅏ is a vertical stick; in 그 the ㄱ sits on top of ㅡ because ㅡ is a horizontal stick.

A final consonant always goes at the bottom of the block: 샘 (ㅅ + ㅐ + ㅁ) and 놀 (ㄴ + ㅗ + ㄹ).

explanations.title: The placeholder ㅇ
explanations.body: When a syllable has no initial consonant (V or VC), a placeholder ㅇ is written in its place, again only for looks. At the start of a syllable ㅇ has no sound of its own, so 오 and 이 sound exactly like ㅗ and ㅣ.

explanations.title: Counting syllables
explanations.body: To count the syllables in a word, count the blocks. The book gives 가족 (2 syllables) as its worked example and asks you to count the rest; the counts below are mine. The meanings are also mine, because the book does not give them.

rows: Always take care with fire (a fire-safety slogan)
The rose of Sharon has bloomed (the title of a children’s game)

exercises.prompt: What shape is the syllable 가?
exercises.explanation: 가 = ㄱ + ㅏ, so it is CV.

exercises.prompt: What shape is the syllable 엄?
exercises.explanation: 엄 = ㅇ + ㅓ + ㅁ, so it is VC.

exercises.prompt: What shape is the syllable 샘?
exercises.explanation: 샘 = ㅅ + ㅐ + ㅁ, so it is CVC.

exercises.prompt: What shape is the syllable 오?
exercises.explanation: 오 = ㅇ + ㅗ, so it is V.

exercises.prompt: What shape is the syllable 놀?
exercises.explanation: 놀 = ㄴ + ㅗ + ㄹ, so it is CVC.

exercises.prompt: What shape is the syllable 꽃?
exercises.explanation: 꽃 = ㄲ + ㅗ + ㅊ, so it is CVC.

exercises.prompt: What shape is the syllable 인?
exercises.explanation: 인 = ㅇ + ㅣ + ㄴ, so it is VC.

exercises.prompt: What shape is the syllable 그?
exercises.explanation: 그 = ㄱ + ㅡ, so it is CV.

exercises.prompt: Is the vowel in 가 a vertical or a horizontal stick?
exercises.explanation: The vowel of 가 is ㅏ, a vertical stick.

exercises.prompt: Is the vowel in 소 a vertical or a horizontal stick?
exercises.explanation: The vowel of 소 is ㅗ, a horizontal stick.

exercises.prompt: Is the vowel in 두 a vertical or a horizontal stick?
exercises.explanation: The vowel of 두 is ㅜ, a horizontal stick.

exercises.prompt: Is the vowel in 인 a vertical or a horizontal stick?
exercises.explanation: The vowel of 인 is ㅣ, a vertical stick.

exercises.prompt: Where does the initial consonant go next to a vertical-stick vowel such as ㅏ?
options: To the left of the vowel
exercises.explanation: With a vertical stick the consonant goes on the left (가); with a horizontal stick it goes on top (그).

exercises.prompt: Where does a final consonant go in a syllable block?
exercises.explanation: The final consonant is always at the bottom of the block, as the ㅁ in 샘.

exercises.prompt: What does the placeholder ㅇ sound like at the start of a syllable?
exercises.explanation: At the start of a syllable ㅇ has no sound; it only fills the empty place, so 오 sounds like ㅗ.

explanations.title: Eight simple vowels
explanations.body: Korean has eight simple vowels: ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ, ㅣ, ㅐ and ㅔ. In this lesson you learn the first six. (The book’s sound clips, mouth-shape videos and writing practice cannot be included; tap a syllable to hear it.)

tables.note: The romanization column is the Revised Romanization used by Korean road signs and dictionaries; it is a spelling convention, not an English approximation.

explanations.title: Vowels written with the placeholder
explanations.body: A vowel on its own is written with the silent placeholder ㅇ in front, so each of the six becomes a syllable. Tap each one.

exercises.prompt: Which vowel sounds like the “a” in father?
exercises.explanation: ㅏ sounds like the “a” in father.

exercises.prompt: Which vowel sounds like the “u” in sun or null?
exercises.explanation: ㅓ sounds like the “u” in sun or null (romanized eo).

exercises.prompt: Which vowel sounds like the “o” in north?
exercises.explanation: ㅗ sounds like the “o” in north or Noriega.

exercises.prompt: Which vowel sounds like the “oo” in too?
exercises.explanation: ㅜ sounds like the “oo” in too or soothe.

exercises.prompt: Which vowel has no close English sound?
exercises.explanation: No English sound approximates ㅡ (romanized eu).

exercises.prompt: Which vowel sounds like the “ee” in teen or feet?
exercises.explanation: ㅣ sounds like the “ee” in teen or feet.

lessons.title: 4. Consonants ㄱ and ㄴ
lessons.subtitle: 기역 · 니은 · 가 거 고 구 그 기 · 나 너 노 누 느 니

explanations.title: ㄱ (기역)
explanations.body:
ㄱ is named 기역 and is said in two ways.

1. At the beginning of a word it has a k-like sound. The first ㄱ in 고기 (meat) is like the “c” in cool or the “k” in kiss, but, unlike the English c or k, it is not followed by a heavy puff of air.
2. Between vowels it has a g-like sound. The second ㄱ in 고기 is like the “g” in go or good.

ㄱ changes its shape a little for looks, depending on whether the vowel is a vertical or a horizontal stick; compare 가 and 그.

examples.translation: gogi — meat

explanations.title: ㄴ (니은)
explanations.body: ㄴ is named 니은 and is said like the “n” in nice or no.

exercises.prompt: What is the name of the letter ㄱ?
What is the name of the letter ㄴ?

exercises.explanation: 기역 is the name of ㄱ.
니은 is the name of ㄴ.

exercises.prompt: Where is ㄱ said like the “g” in go?
options: At the beginning of a word
exercises.explanation: Between vowels ㄱ is g-like, as the second ㄱ of 고기.

exercises.prompt: How is ㄱ said at the beginning of a word?
options: Like a k with a strong puff of air
Like a k, but without a heavy puff of air
exercises.explanation: At the beginning of a word ㄱ is k-like but not accompanied by a heavy puff of air, unlike the English c or k.

exercises.prompt: Which English word has the sound of ㄴ?
exercises.explanation: ㄴ is said like the “n” in nice or no.

exercises.prompt: Why does ㄱ look slightly different in 가 and 그?
options: Its shape adjusts to a vertical or a horizontal stick vowel
exercises.explanation: ㄱ changes shape a little for looks, depending on the vowel it is written with.

lessons.title: 5. Consonants ㄷ and ㄹ
lessons.subtitle: 디귿 · 리을 · 다 더 도 두 드 디 · 라 러 로 루 르 리

explanations.title: ㄷ (디귿)
explanations.body:
ㄷ is named 디귿 and is said in two ways.

1. At the beginning of a word it has a t-like sound. The ㄷ in 다리 (leg; bridge) is like the “t” in tall and team, but, unlike the English t, it is not followed by a heavy puff of air.
2. Between vowels, or between some voiced consonants, it has a d-like sound. The ㄷ in 구두 (shoes) is like the “d” in do or day.

examples.translation: dari — leg; bridge
gudu — shoes

explanations.title: ㄹ (리을)
explanations.body:
ㄹ is named 리을 and is said in two ways.

1. At the beginning of a word, or at the end of a syllable, it has an l-like sound: the ㄹ in 라면 (ramen noodles) and 발 (foot) is like the “l” in lady or long. The tip of the tongue touches the palate, not the back of the teeth.
2. Between vowels it is a “flap”: the ㄹ in 나라 (nation) or 도로 (street; road) sounds something like the “t” in water or the “tt” in latter.

A flap is made with a single quick contraction of the muscles, so that the tongue is thrown against the roof of the mouth. The “t” in batter or quarter is a flap when an unstressed vowel follows it.

examples.translation: ramyeon — ramen noodles
bal — foot
nara — nation
doro — street; road

exercises.prompt: What is the name of the letter ㄷ?
What is the name of the letter ㄹ?

exercises.explanation: 디귿 is the name of ㄷ.
리을 is the name of ㄹ.

exercises.prompt: Where is ㄷ said like the “d” in do?
options: At the end of a word
At the beginning of a word
exercises.explanation: Between vowels (or some voiced consonants) ㄷ is d-like, as in 구두.

exercises.prompt: How is ㄷ said at the beginning of a word?
options: Like a t, but without a heavy puff of air
Like a t with a strong puff of air
exercises.explanation: At the start of a word ㄷ is t-like, as in 다리, without the heavy puff of the English t.

exercises.prompt: How is ㄹ said at the beginning of a word, as in 라면?
exercises.explanation: At the start of a word, and at the end of a syllable, ㄹ is l-like.

exercises.prompt: How is ㄹ said between vowels, as in 나라?
options: Like an l with the tongue on the teeth
As a flap, something like the “tt” in latter
exercises.explanation: Between vowels ㄹ is a flap, similar to the t in water.

exercises.prompt: Where does the tip of the tongue touch when you say the l-like ㄹ?
exercises.explanation: For ㄹ the tongue tip touches the palate, not the back of the teeth.

lessons.title: 7. Saying hello
lessons.subtitle: 안녕하세요? · 만나서 반갑습니다 · 성함이 어떻게 되십니까?

explanations.title: Greeting and introducing yourself
explanations.body: These are the first six expressions of the course. Practice them aloud, then use them with a partner. The book’s example answers are 김민수입니다 (the name of the person speaking is Kim Minsoo) and 시카고입니다 or 서울입니다 for the hometown. In a real conversation you replace the name and the place with your own, followed by 입니다. The book explains the grammar in later lessons.

examples.translation: annyeonghaseyo? — How are you? / Hello.
mannaseo bangapseumnida. — Nice to meet you.
seonghami eotteoke doesimnikka? — What is your name?
gimminsuimnida. — My name is Kim Minsoo.
gohyangi eodisimnikka? — Where is your hometown?
sikagoimnida. — My hometown is Chicago.
seourimnida. — I’m from Seoul. / My hometown is Seoul.

explanations.title: A first meeting
explanations.body: Putting the expressions together, a first meeting goes like this (the order is the book’s; the speaker labels 가 and 나 stand for A and B).

examples.translation: ga: annyeonghaseyo? — How are you? / Hello.
na: annyeonghaseyo? mannaseo bangapseumnida. — Hello. Nice to meet you.
ga: seonghami eotteoke doesimnikka? — What is your name?
na: gimminsuimnida. — My name is Kim Minsoo.
ga: gohyangi eodisimnikka? — Where is your hometown?
na: seourimnida. — I’m from Seoul.

lessons.title: 9. Two more simple vowels: ㅐ and ㅔ
lessons.subtitle: 애 에 · 개 내 대 래 · 게 네 데 레

explanations.title: ㅐ and ㅔ
explanations.body:
In Lesson 1 you learned six of the eight simple vowels. The last two are ㅐ and ㅔ.

ㅐ is made up of ㅏ and ㅣ. It sounds like the “a” in apple or sad.
ㅔ is made up of ㅓ and ㅣ. It sounds like the “e” in bed or elk.

Unlike English, the difference in sound between ㅐ and ㅔ is not clear: the two sound very much alike, so you will learn which one a word uses by learning the word itself.

exercises.prompt: Which vowel is made up of ㅏ and ㅣ?
exercises.explanation: ㅐ is ㅏ + ㅣ; ㅔ is ㅓ + ㅣ.

exercises.prompt: Which vowel is made up of ㅓ and ㅣ?
Which vowel sounds like the “a” in apple or sad?
exercises.explanation: ㅐ sounds like the “a” in apple or sad.

exercises.prompt: Which vowel sounds like the “e” in bed or elk?
exercises.explanation: ㅔ sounds like the “e” in bed or elk.

exercises.prompt: How clear is the difference in sound between ㅐ and ㅔ?
options: Not clear: they sound very much alike
ㅐ is much longer than ㅔ
exercises.explanation: Unlike English, the sound distinction between ㅐ and ㅔ is not clear.

lessons.title: 10. Y-vowels: ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ
lessons.subtitle: 야 여 요 유 · 갸 겨 교 규

explanations.title: Six y-vowels
explanations.body:
Korean has six y-vowels: ㅑ, ㅕ, ㅛ, ㅠ, ㅒ and ㅖ. They are called y-vowels because each sounds like a vowel preceded by a y, as in young, yodel, you, yell. In writing, the two dots, or two small sticks, stand for that y sound.

You make a y-vowel by adding a second small stick to a simple vowel: ㅏ → ㅑ, ㅓ → ㅕ, ㅗ → ㅛ, ㅜ → ㅠ, ㅐ → ㅒ, ㅔ → ㅖ. In this lesson you learn the first four; ㅒ and ㅖ come in the next lesson.

lessons.title: 11. Consonants ㅁ and ㅂ

explanations.title: ㅁ (미음)
explanations.body: ㅁ is named 미음 and is said like the “m” in map or team.

explanations.title: ㅂ (비읍)
explanations.body:
ㅂ is named 비읍 and is said in two ways.

1. At the beginning of a word it has a p-like sound. The ㅂ in 바다 (sea) is like the “p” in pen, but, unlike the English p, it is not followed by a heavy puff of air.
2. Between vowels it has a b-like sound. The ㅂ in 두부 (tofu) is like the “b” in boy.

lessons.title: 12. Consonants ㅅ ㅈ ㅎ
lessons.subtitle: 시옷 · 지읒 · 히읗 · 지도 · 기자

explanations.title: ㅅ (시옷)
explanations.body:
ㅅ is named 시옷. It is said like the “s” before an unstressed vowel, as in significant or secure. When ㅅ is followed by the vowel ㅣ, Koreans often say it like the “sh” in she.

The romanization still writes 시 as si.

rows: 사 샤 소 쇼 수 슈

explanations.title: ㅈ (지읒)
explanations.body:
ㅈ is named 지읒 and is said in two ways.

1. At the beginning of a word it has a ch-like sound. The ㅈ in 지도 (map) is like the “ch” in child, but, unlike the English ch, it is not followed by a heavy puff of air.
2. Between vowels it has a j-like sound. The ㅈ in 기자 (reporter) is like the “j” in joy.

jae jeo je jo ju jeu

explanations.title: ㅎ (히읗)
explanations.body: ㅎ is named 히읗 and is said like the “h” in half and have.

explanations.title: Saying thank you and answering
explanations.body: 감사합니다 and 고맙습니다 both mean “Thank you.” The answers are 천만에요 (“You’re welcome”) and 아이, 아닙니다 (“Don’t mention it”). The book lists these four in this order and asks you to match each to “You’re welcome”, “Thank you” or “Don’t mention it”; one of them can take more than one answer. The two answers mean much the same thing, so either can be translated “You’re welcome” (that reading is mine).

lessons.title: 16. W-vowels: ㅘ ㅝ ㅚ ㅟ
lessons.subtitle: 와 워 외 위 · 과 궈 괴 귀

explanations.title: Six w-vowels
explanations.body:
Korean has six w-vowels: ㅘ, ㅝ, ㅚ, ㅟ, ㅙ and ㅞ. They are called w-vowels because they begin with an English w sound, as in watt, win, week, wet, world. In writing, a w-vowel is ㅗ or ㅜ combined with ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅣ, ㅐ or ㅔ: ㅘ, ㅝ, ㅚ, ㅟ, ㅙ, ㅞ.

To say one, sound the two vowels quickly one after the other, as if they were one sound. Say ㅗ and ㅏ quickly and you say 와. This lesson has the first four; ㅙ and ㅞ come in Lesson 4.

rows: the “we” in wet or Wendy (though it is made of ㅗ and ㅣ)

lessons.title: 17. The vowel ㅢ
lessons.subtitle: 의 · 희 · 늬

explanations.title: ㅢ
explanations.body:
ㅢ is made up of ㅡ and ㅣ. Saying the two quickly together gives a sound that, unfortunately, has no English equivalent.

When ㅢ comes after any consonant other than the placeholder ㅇ (as in 늬 or 희), it loses the ㅡ sound: 늬 sounds the same as 니, and 희 sounds the same as 히. Only when it starts the syllable on its own, as in 의, do you hear the full ㅡ + ㅣ sound.

A note on romanization (mine): the Revised Romanization always writes ㅢ as ui, even where it is said like ㅣ, so 희 is romanized hui although it sounds like 히.

exercises.explanation: The book says the sound unfortunately has no English equivalent.

lessons.title: 18. Aspirated consonants: ㅊ ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ
lessons.subtitle: 치읓 · 키읔 · 티읕 · 피읖

explanations.title: Plain and aspirated
explanations.body:
In the earlier lessons you learned the plain consonants ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ and ㅈ. Now you learn their aspirated counterparts ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ and ㅊ, which are said with a heavy puff of air. In writing, the puff of air is shown by a dot or a little stick added to the plain letter; ㅍ is the exception.

To practise, hold a piece of paper in front of your mouth. If the paper moves, you have said the aspirated sound correctly; if it does not, you have said the plain counterpart (ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ or ㅈ).

explanations.body: The names and sounds, each with a heavy puff of air.

lessons.title: 23. Two more y-vowels: ㅒ ㅖ
lessons.subtitle: 얘 · 걔 · 쟤 · 예 · 계 · 폐

explanations.title: ㅒ and ㅖ
explanations.body:
You already know four y-vowels (ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ). Lesson 4 adds the other two, ㅒ and ㅖ.

ㅒ sounds like the “ya” in yank. You make it by adding a y sound to 애.

ㅖ sounds like the “ye” in yes. You make it by adding a y sound to 에.

Unlike the other y-vowels, ㅒ loses its y sound when it comes after any consonant other than ㅅ: 걔 sounds the same as 개, and 쟤 sounds the same as 재. ㅖ loses its y sound after a consonant too: 계 sounds the same as 게, and 폐 sounds the same as 페. As with ㅐ and ㅔ, it is hard to tell ㅒ and ㅖ apart.

Note: 섀 appears only in a loanword such as 섀도 마스크 (shadow mask), so it sounds like the “sha” in shadow.

rows: the same as 헤 (by the same rule)

explanations.title: Spelling and sound (mine)
explanations.body: The Revised Romanization spells ㅒ and ㅖ with the y even where it is not said, the same way it spells 희 as hui although it is said 히. So 걔 is written gyae and 계 is written gye, but they are said like 개 and 게. With the placeholder ㅇ (얘, 예) the y is kept. After ㅈ the romanization drops the y (쟤 is jae), as it does for 져 (jeo).

explanations.title: ㅙ and ㅞ
explanations.body:
You already know four w-vowels (ㅘ ㅝ ㅚ ㅟ). Lesson 4 adds the last two, ㅙ and ㅞ.

ㅙ is made up of ㅗ and ㅐ. Said quickly, the two vowels sound like the “wa” in wagon. Keep in mind that ㅙ sounds the same as the vowel ㅚ from Lesson 3.

ㅞ is made up of ㅜ and ㅔ. Said quickly, the two vowels sound like the “wea” in weapon or the “we” in Wendy. As with ㅐ and ㅔ, the sound distinction between ㅙ and ㅞ is not clear. Keep in mind that the three vowels ㅙ, ㅚ and ㅞ sound the same.

lessons.title: 25. Double consonants: ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ
lessons.subtitle: 까 · 따 · 빠 · 쌍기역 · 쌍디귿 · 쌍비읍

explanations.title: Plain, aspirated and double
explanations.body:
ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ and ㅉ are called “double” consonants because they are spelled by doubling ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ and ㅈ. They are also known as “glottal” or “tensed” consonants, because they are produced by holding the throat tense and then releasing the sound without a puff of air.

ㄲ, ㄸ and ㅃ are similar to “k”, “t” and “p” when they immediately follow the consonant “s”, as in sky, star and spy. ㅆ is similar to the “s” sound followed by a stressed vowel, as in sun, soul and silly. The double consonants are easier to understand beside their counterparts.

rows: Plain: ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ ㅅ ㅈ
Aspirated: ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ (none for ㅅ) ㅊ
Double: ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ

explanations.title: ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ
explanations.body: ㄲ is called 쌍기역 and sounds like the “k” in sky or skate. ㄸ is called 쌍디귿 and sounds like the “t” in star or style. ㅃ is called 쌍비읍 and sounds like the “p” in spy or speak.

lessons.title: 29. Looking up words: dictionary order
lessons.subtitle: 가다 · 입다 · ㄲ at the end of ㄱ · ㅐ after ㅏ

explanations.title: Looking up a word
explanations.body: To find “tourist” in an English dictionary you look for t, then o, u, r, i, s, t. Korean works the same way. To look up 가다 you use ㄱ, ㅏ, ㄷ, ㅏ (four steps); to look up 입다 you use ㅇ, ㅣ, ㅂ, ㄷ, ㅏ (five steps, because 입 has a final consonant).

explanations.title: The consonant sequence
explanations.body: The Korean dictionary is organised by consonants. The main sections come in this order: ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅅ ㅇ ㅈ ㅊ ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅎ. The double consonants are at the end of their own sections, so if you are looking up ㄲ you find it at the very end of the ㄱ section.

headers: Its double consonant, at the end of the section

rows: ㄱ ㄲ ㄴ ㄷ ㄸ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅃ ㅅ ㅆ ㅇ ㅈ ㅉ ㅊ ㅋ ㅌ ㅍ ㅎ

explanations.title: The vowel sequence
explanations.body: After the initial consonant, use the vowel sequence. The y-vowels and w-vowels are slotted in beside the vowels they are built on: ㅐ after ㅏ, ㅒ after ㅑ, ㅔ after ㅓ, ㅖ after ㅕ, ㅘ ㅙ ㅚ after ㅗ, ㅝ ㅞ ㅟ after ㅜ, and ㅢ after ㅡ.

rows: ㅏ ㅐ ㅑ ㅒ ㅓ ㅔ ㅕ ㅖ ㅗ ㅘ ㅙ ㅚ ㅛ ㅜ ㅝ ㅞ ㅟ ㅠ ㅡ ㅢ ㅣ

explanations.title: Looking up 가다
explanations.body:
1. Find the ㄱ section. 2. Inside it, use the vowel sequence to find the vowel of the first syllable (ㅏ). 3. In the part for the syllable 가, use the consonant sequence to find the first consonant of the next syllable (ㄷ). 4. In the words that begin with 가ㄷ, use the vowel sequence to find the vowel (ㅏ).

A note (mine): a syllable with no final consonant comes before the same syllable with one, so 가 comes before 간. The book’s activities do not need this, but a real dictionary does.

lessons.title: 30. Loanword rules
lessons.subtitle: 스트라이크 · 뉴욕 · 커피숍 · 파리 · 라디오 · 필름

explanations.title: Spelling English words in Korean
explanations.body: In the past several decades, numerous English words have become part of everyday Korean. That does not make them easy for a native English speaker to recognise, because Koreans spell and pronounce loanwords differently. For example, the one-syllable English word “strike” is spelled 스트라이크, a word of five syllables. These rules of thumb help you recognise loanwords as you learn Korean.

examples.translation: seuteuraikeu — strike

explanations.title: 1. Diphthongs are two vowels
explanations.body: A diphthong is treated as two separate vowel sounds. The exception is the diphthong /ou/ as in boat and note, which becomes one vowel, 오.

explanations.title: 2. A loose consonant gets ㅡ
explanations.body: In Korean a consonant or a vowel cannot stand alone as a syllable. A consonant has to depend on a vowel, directly before or after it. So an extra vowel (ㅡ) is inserted next to any loose consonant or cluster of consonants: s-t-r-aik becomes 스-트-라이-크.

examples.translation: seuteuraikeu — strike

explanations.title: 3. Final consonants: only ㄱ ㄴ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅅ ㅇ
explanations.body: Only ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ and ㅇ can be used at the end of a syllable. So the sounds “k”, “p” and “t” after a vowel in a syllable are spelled ㄱ, ㅂ and ㅅ. The “k” in New York is spelled ㄱ, not ㅋ (뉴욕); the “p” in coffee shop is spelled ㅂ, not ㅍ (커피숍).

explanations.title: 4. No double consonants at the start
explanations.body: The double consonants ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ are not used at the start of a syllable in a loanword, even when the word has a sound like ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ or ㅉ. The “P” of Paris is spelled with ㅍ: 파리 (not 빠리).

examples.translation: pari — Paris (not 빠리)

explanations.title: 5. r and l are both ㄹ
explanations.body: In Korean “r” and “l” are considered the same sound and are both spelled ㄹ. However, an “r” after a vowel, as in card or computer, is silent. When an “l” has a consonant before or after it, as in slide and film, it is often spelled ㄹㄹ.

explanations.title: 6. Vowels that need attention
explanations.body: The “a” of California is associated with ㅐ and the “e” of Minnesota with ㅔ. Because of the influence of British English, “o” tends to be associated with ㅗ.

explanations.title: 7. Sounds Korean does not have
explanations.body: Sounds that do not exist in Korean are approximated by the closest Korean sounds. The “th” of theme or Thatcher becomes ㅅ, ㅌ or ㄷ. The “f” of film and file becomes ㅍ or ㅎ; fitness can be 피트니스 or 휘트니스.

explanations.title: 8. Loanwords from other languages
explanations.body: For loanwords that come from other languages, the local pronunciation is reflected: Paris (French) is 파리, and arbeit (German, “part-time work”) is 아르바이트.

exercises.prompt: How is the English word “strike” spelled in Korean?
exercises.explanation: 스트라이크 has five syllables because a vowel (ㅡ) is added to loose consonants.

exercises.prompt: How does Korean treat a diphthong such as the one in “house”?
exercises.explanation: Diphthongs are treated as two separate vowel sounds: 하우스.

exercises.prompt: Which diphthong is the exception, becoming one vowel (오)?
exercises.explanation: The diphthong /ou/ becomes one vowel, 오: 보트, 노트.

exercises.prompt: Which extra vowel is inserted next to a loose consonant in a loanword?
exercises.explanation: An extra ㅡ is inserted, as in 스트라이크.

exercises.prompt: Which final consonants can a loanword syllable use?
options: ㄱ ㄴ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅅ ㅇ
exercises.explanation: Only ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅅ and ㅇ can end a syllable.

exercises.prompt: How is the “k” in New York spelled at the end of a syllable?
exercises.explanation: The “k” is spelled ㄱ, not ㅋ: 뉴욕.

exercises.prompt: How is the “p” in coffee shop spelled at the end of a syllable?
exercises.explanation: The “p” is spelled ㅂ, not ㅍ: 커피숍.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is the loanword for “Paris”?
exercises.explanation: The P of Paris is spelled ㅍ; double consonants are not used at the start of a loanword syllable: 파리, not 빠리.

exercises.prompt: Are double consonants (ㄲ ㄸ ㅃ ㅆ ㅉ) used at the start of a syllable in loanwords?
options: Only at the end of a word
No, not even when the sound seems close
exercises.explanation: The double consonants are not used syllable-initially in loanwords: 파리, not 빠리.

exercises.prompt: How are the English sounds “r” and “l” spelled in Korean?
options: r is ㅇ and l is ㄹ
r is ㄹ and l is ㄴ
exercises.explanation: Korean treats r and l as the same sound, spelled ㄹ.

exercises.prompt: What happens to the “r” after a vowel, as in card?
exercises.explanation: An “r” after a vowel is silent: 카드.

exercises.prompt: How is the “l” often spelled when a consonant comes before or after it, as in slide and film?
The “a” of California is associated with which vowel?
exercises.explanation: The “a” is associated with ㅐ: 캘리포니아.

exercises.prompt: The “e” of Minnesota is associated with which vowel?
exercises.explanation: The “e” is associated with ㅔ: 미네소타.

exercises.prompt: The “o” of Boston tends to be associated with which vowel?
exercises.explanation: Because of the influence of British English, “o” tends to be ㅗ: 보스턴.

exercises.prompt: Which Korean sounds approximate the English “th”?
exercises.explanation: The “th” of theme and Thatcher becomes ㅅ, ㅌ or ㄷ: 테마, 대처.

exercises.prompt: Which Korean sounds approximate the English “f”?
exercises.explanation: The “f” of film and file becomes ㅍ or ㅎ: 필름, 파일, 휘트니스.

exercises.prompt: How are loanwords from French or German pronounced?
exercises.explanation: Paris (French) is 파리 and arbeit (German) is 아르바이트.
아르바이트 comes from the German arbeit and means part-time work.

lessons.title: 33. Saying good-bye
lessons.subtitle: 안녕히 가세요 · 안녕히 계세요 · 내일 봐요 · 주말 잘 보내세요

explanations.title: Four ways to part
explanations.body: The book teaches two ways of saying “good-bye” and two ways of parting for a while. The two good-byes differ by whom you are speaking to. The book glosses them literally: “Go in peace” and “Stay in peace”. (What follows is mine: you say “go in peace” to the person who is leaving, and “stay in peace” to the person who is staying behind.)

examples.translation: annyeonghi gaseyo. — Good-bye; “Go in peace.”
annyeonghi gyeseyo. — Good-bye; “Stay in peace.”
naeil bwayo. — See you tomorrow.

explanations.title: A parting, from both sides (mine)
explanations.body: The pairing is mine; the book gives only the four expressions. The person who stays says “go in peace” to the person who leaves, who answers “stay in peace”.

lessons.title: 35. Final consonants: only seven sounds
lessons.subtitle: 악 안 앋 알 암 압 앙 · ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ merge

explanations.title: Consonants at the end of a syllable
explanations.body:
So far you have met the 14 basic consonants and 5 double consonants as initial consonants, the ones that come at the beginning of a syllable. With the exception of ㄸ, ㅃ and ㅉ, all of them can also be used as final consonants (batchim), written under the vowel. For example:

악 안 앋 알 암 압 앗 앙 앚 앛 앜 앝 앞 앟 앆 았

In speech, however, only seven final consonants keep their sound value: ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ and ㅇ. All the others merge into three of these seven sounds.

rows: ㄷ, ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅌ, ㅎ

headers: Romanization at the end of a syllable

explanations.title: Same place in the mouth
explanations.body: The merging consonants use similar places of articulation. For example, ㄱ, ㄲ and ㅋ are all velar consonants, that is, consonants made with the back of the tongue against the soft palate, so they all end up as the same ㄱ sound.

explanations.title: The sixteen syllables with ㅇ (as the book writes them)
explanations.body: Each syllable below is the vowel ㅏ with a different final consonant. Notice which ones are said alike.

explanations.title: A note on romanization (mine)
explanations.body: The Revised Romanization writes the sound that is actually said: a final ㄱ, ㄲ or ㅋ is k; a final ㄷ, ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅌ or ㅎ is t; a final ㅂ or ㅍ is p; a final ㄹ is l; and a final ㅇ is ng. So 앞 is ap and 앟 is at.

exercises.prompt: How many final consonants keep their own sound in speech?

lessons.title: 36. Final ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ: the unreleased k, t, p
lessons.subtitle: 막 밖 엌 · 갔 꽃 낮 · 곱 덮 숲

explanations.title: The /k/ group: ㄱ, ㄲ, ㅋ
explanations.body: These consonants all sound like the “k” in book or cheek. Unlike the English sound, however, it is not released. They have a short, flat sound: the mouth closes on the sound and stops.

explanations.title: The /t/ group: ㄷ, ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅌ, ㅎ
explanations.body: These consonants all sound like the “t” in cat, again without the release of the English sound: a short, flat sound.

explanations.title: The /p/ group: ㅂ, ㅍ
explanations.body: These consonants all sound like the “p” in tip or keep, again not released: a short, flat sound.

explanations.title: Which letter is written? (mine)
explanations.body: The letters written under the vowel in the examples are: 막 ㄱ, 밖 ㄲ, 엌 ㅋ, 책 ㄱ; 갔 ㅆ, 꽃 ㅊ, 낮 ㅈ, 밑 ㅌ, 옷 ㅅ, 얗 ㅎ; 곱 ㅂ, 덮 ㅍ, 숲 ㅍ, 탑 ㅂ. You cannot tell the letter from the sound, so you have to learn the spelling of each word.

lessons.title: 40. Sino-Korean numbers 0–100

explanations.title: Two number systems
explanations.body: There are two number systems in Korean: Sino-Korean numbers and native (or pure) Korean numbers. Sino-Korean refers to the set of numbers that originated from, or were influenced by, the Chinese language. This lesson has the Sino-Korean numbers; the native numbers are introduced in a later lesson (Lesson 6).

explanations.title: 0 to 9
explanations.body: The book gives two forms for 6, 육 and 륙; the numbers below use 육.

explanations.title: 10 to 100
explanations.body: Ten, twenty and so on up to one hundred.

explanations.title: Building the other numbers
explanations.body:
In this numbering system, 45 is considered as 4 × 10 + 5, so 45 reads 사십오. All other two-digit numbers read in this way: 21 is 2 × 10 + 1, 이십일; 99 is 구십구.

A note (mine): for 10 to 19 you say just 십, 십일, 십이…, with no 일 before 십; 17 is 십칠, not 일십칠. Some of the sound changes you learned apply too: 십 plus 일 is said 시빌, 십 plus 육 is said 심뉵 (16), and 십 plus 구 is said 십꾸.

lessons.title: 44. The sound-linking rule
lessons.subtitle: 단어 → 다너 · 군인 → 구닌 · 한국어 → 한구거

explanations.title: Carried over, in English and in Korean
explanations.body:
Say these English phrases at normal speed: “Stop it!” and “She baked it.” They sound like “Sto pit” and “She bake dit”. This is because the “p” in stop and the “d” in baked are “carried over” to the word it. The same thing happens in Korean.

Whenever a syllable ends in a consonant and the next syllable starts with a vowel, the final consonant is carried over to the next syllable. This is known as the sound-linking rule, or the consonant carry-over rule. In the book’s picture, the ㄴ at the end of the first syllable of 단어 moves to the second syllable, so the word sounds like 다너. (The picture is not reproduced; the English for 단어 is mine.)

explanations.title: Reading the pronunciation
explanations.body: The Revised Romanization follows what is said, so it shows the carried consonant at the start of the next syllable: 군인 is gunin and 한국어 is hangugeo. A note (mine): a final ㅇ (ng) is never carried over, so a word such as 송아지 (songaji) is said as it is written.

exercises.explanation: A final consonant moves to the next syllable if that syllable starts with ㅇ (a vowel sound).

lessons.title: 45. Final consonant clusters
lessons.subtitle: 앉 않 닭 맑 읽 젊 넓 옳 잃 없

explanations.title: Eleven clusters, one sound
explanations.body: There are 11 consonant clusters that come at the end of a syllable: ㄳ, ㄵ, ㄶ, ㄺ, ㄻ, ㄼ, ㄽ, ㄾ, ㄿ, ㅀ and ㅄ. Although these clusters are made up of two different consonants, they have only one sound value. In other words, one of the consonants is silent. The next tables show which one. In this lesson you practise ㄵ, ㄶ, ㄺ, ㄻ, ㄼ, ㅀ and ㅄ; syllables that end in the other clusters are practised later in the course. (The one example for each cluster is taken from the book’s tables.)

explanations.title: The second consonant is silent
explanations.body: In ㄳ, ㄵ, ㄶ, ㄼ, ㄽ, ㄾ, ㅀ and ㅄ, the second consonant is silent. The book prints these examples with the sound between slashes (the meanings are not given).

explanations.title: The first consonant is silent
explanations.body: In ㄺ, ㄻ and ㄿ, the first consonant is silent. The book prints 읊 as /읖/; since a final ㅍ is said ㅂ, the table below writes the sound as 읍.

explanations.title: Exceptions
explanations.body: There are a few exceptions to the rules above. In the case of 밟, as in 밟다 (to tread), the ㄹ is silent: 밟 is said 밥. And when ㄺ is part of a verb and it is followed by the consonant ㄱ, the ㄱ is silent: 맑게 is said 말께 and 밝게 is said 발께. (The meanings of 맑게 and 밝게 are mine.)

explanations.title: When a vowel follows
explanations.body: When these consonant clusters are followed by a vowel, their second consonant is carried over to the next syllable and both consonants are pronounced. Compare 삶 (said 삼) with 삶으세요 (said 살므세요): the same cluster, but now both ㄹ and ㅁ are heard. (The book gives no meanings; the English below is mine.)

explanations.title: The exception: ㅎ stays silent
explanations.body: However, if the second consonant is ㅎ, it is not carried over to the next syllable and remains silent. So the first consonant is the one that is carried over.

explanations.title: Putting the rules together (mine)
explanations.body: A cluster at the end of a word or before a consonant has one sound, and the same cluster before a vowel has two. The words below are from the book’s sentences; “said” shows both cases.

explanations.title: The native numbers
explanations.body: Below are the native (or pure) Korean numbers. Unlike the Sino-Korean system, 20, 30, 40 and so forth have unique names. Therefore 46 is considered 40 + 6 and reads 마흔여섯. Listen to the numbers and repeat them aloud several times. (The recording is not included.)

explanations.title: Building the other numbers
explanations.body: As in the Sino-Korean system, the other numbers are the ten plus the one: 46 is 40 + 6 = 마흔여섯; 99 is 90 + 9 = 아흔아홉. A note (mine): for 11, 12 … say 열하나, 열둘 …, and for 21, 22 … say 스물하나, 스물둘 …. The book stops at 99, and its native numbers have no word for 100.

explanations.title: Sound changes in some numbers (mine)
explanations.body: The book teaches only how the numbers are built. In speech, an ㄴ or ㄹ is added when a ten is followed by 여섯, 일곱 or 여덟: 열여섯 is said 열려섣, 서른일곱 is said 서른닐곱. The romanization follows what is said. With 아홉 the consonant is carried over, as in Lesson 6: 열아홉 is said 여라홉.

explanations.body: Compare the two systems for the same number. Which one to use depends on what you are counting; the book introduces that later.

units.title: Appendix: sound rules and Korean vocabulary

lessons.title: 51. Assimilation: three directions
lessons.subtitle: 앞문 → 암문 · 칼날 → 칼랄 · 백로 → 뱅노

explanations.title: Salient Korean phonological rules
explanations.body: The Appendix covers several salient Korean phonological rules that Korean language learners must be familiar with. Understanding the rules will help you not only to pronounce Korean more naturally but also to understand, with less effort, what Koreans say.

explanations.title: What assimilation is
explanations.body: Assimilation is a sound change due to the influence of an adjoining sound. It is a universal phenomenon. In Korean, assimilation occurs in consonants when a “dominant” consonant adjoins another consonant. Assimilation occurs in three different directions: backward, forward and reciprocal.

explanations.title: Backward, forward, reciprocal
explanations.body: Backward assimilation: being influenced by a following consonant, the preceding consonant is assimilated. Forward assimilation: being influenced by a preceding consonant, the following consonant is assimilated. Reciprocal assimilation: two neighboring consonants are assimilated because of their mutual influence. The book shows one word for each in a picture, with the changed sounds marked.

explanations.title: Three categories
explanations.body: Depending on the type of sound change, we can place assimilation into three categories: (1) nasalization, (2) ㄴ to ㄹ assimilation, and (3) assimilation of the “stop sound” before ㄹ. The next lessons take them in turn, followed by the other sound changes of the Appendix.

explanations.title: Which direction? (mine)
explanations.body: The book labels only the three words above. The other examples of the Appendix can be sorted in the same way: look at which of the two neighboring consonants changes.

options: A sound change due to the influence of an adjoining sound
A word borrowed from another language
exercises.explanation: Assimilation is defined as a sound change due to the influence of an adjoining sound.

lessons.title: 52. Nasalization
lessons.subtitle: 입니다 → 임니다 · 받는다 → 반는다 · 석면 → 성면 · 담력 → 담녁

explanations.title: Nasal consonants are powerful
explanations.body: ㄴ, ㅁ and ㅇ are nasal consonants, which are powerful “sound change agents.” (Nasal consonants are produced while the velum, or soft palate, is lowered so that some air escapes through the nose.) Whenever a stop sound like ㄱ, ㄷ or ㅂ precedes one of these nasal consonants, it is nasalized into ㅇ, ㄴ or ㅁ. (A stop sound is characterized by the momentary blocking of some part of the oral cavity; ㄱ, ㄷ and ㅂ are typical stop sounds.) Also note that ㄹ is nasalized to ㄴ when it is preceded by a nasal consonant.

rows: A syllable-final stop is followed by a nasal sound
ㅂ → ㅁ, ㄷ → ㄴ, ㄱ → ㅇ
Syllable-final ㅁ or ㅇ precedes ㄹ

explanations.title: The words of the book’s table
explanations.body: Say each word and repeat it several times. (The recording is not included.) Remember from Lesson 5 that the other final consonants are first said as ㄱ, ㄷ or ㅂ: ㅍ is said ㅂ; ㅌ, ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ and ㅎ are said ㄷ; ㅋ and ㄲ are said ㄱ. So 앞문 is first 압문 and then 암문. (The book gives no English; none is added.)

lessons.title: 53. ㄴ to ㄹ, and a stop before ㄹ

explanations.title: ㄴ to ㄹ assimilation
explanations.body: When ㄴ comes before or after ㄹ, the ㄴ sound changes into the ㄹ sound because of the influence of the consonant ㄹ, as in 신라 (said 실라) and 칼날 (said 칼랄). Say each word and repeat it several times. (The recording is not included.)

tables.title: When ㄹ comes before or after ㄴ

explanations.title: The stop sound before ㄹ
explanations.body: When a stop consonant such as ㄱ, ㄷ or ㅂ comes before ㄹ, the stop sound is nasalized into ㅇ, ㄴ or ㅁ. Then the ㄹ sound is in turn also nasalized because of the influence of the new nasalized sound. So the change takes two steps, which the book prints for each word. (The book prints 몇 리 and its sounds without a space.)

explanations.title: Why this is reciprocal (mine)
explanations.body: In the three words above both consonants change: the stop becomes a nasal, and ㄹ becomes ㄴ. That is the reciprocal assimilation of the first lesson. In 난로 and 신라 only the first consonant changes (backward); in 칼날 only the second (forward).

exercises.explanation: ㄴ changes into ㄹ under the influence of ㄹ: 신라 is said 실라.
ㄴ before ㄹ becomes ㄹ: 실라 (silla).
ㄴ after ㄹ becomes ㄹ: 칼랄 (kallal).

ㄷ becomes ㅇ and ㄹ becomes ㄴ

options: ㅂ becomes ㅁ and ㄹ becomes ㄴ
ㅂ becomes ㄴ and ㄹ becomes ㅁ
exercises.explanation: ㅂ + ㄹ → ㅁ + ㄴ: 섭리 is said 섬니.

lessons.title: 54. Adding ㄴ or ㄹ

explanations.title: An extra consonant
explanations.body: When a syllable ends in a consonant and is followed by ㅣ or a y-vowel (ㅑ, ㅕ, ㅛ, ㅠ), the ㄴ or ㄹ sound is inserted between the consonant and the following vowel, respectively: ㄴ is added after a syllable-final stop consonant (or ㄴ), and ㄹ after a syllable-final ㄹ. Say each word and repeat it several times. (The recording is not included.) The book prints 꽃잎 in two steps, /꼳입/ and then /꼰닙/: the inserted ㄴ follows ㄷ, which is then nasalized.

explanations.title: More examples (mine)
explanations.body: Words from the standard pronunciation rules that follow the same pattern, including the native numbers of Lesson 6.

exercises.prompt: When is an extra ㄴ or ㄹ added?

lessons.title: 55. Tensification

explanations.title: Tense after another consonant
explanations.body: In English, we pronounce k, p and t more tensely when they are preceded by s, as in stop, sky and spy. We can observe a similar phenomenon in Korean. The consonants ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ and ㅈ become ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ and ㅉ, respectively, when they follow another stop, a nasal sound, or ㄹ. Say each word and repeat it several times. (The recording is not included.) The Revised Romanization does not show this change: 학교 is hakgyo. (The column “after” is mine.)

explanations.title: Exceptions
explanations.body: There are several exceptions to the tensification rule, as shown in 월부, 팔고, 단발 and 헌병. The book gives only the audio for them; a note (mine): in these words the consonant after ㄹ or ㄴ is not tensified, so the words are said as they are written.

explanations.title: The spelling you cannot see (mine)
explanations.body: Many words are written with a plain consonant but said with a tense one, so the tense sound is not in the spelling. When you read, remember that ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ and ㅈ after a final stop are tense, as in 학교 (학꾜).

lessons.title: 56. Aspiration
lessons.subtitle: 않고 → 안코 · 좋지 → 조치 · 각하 → 가카 · 입학 → 이팍

explanations.title: ㅎ joins the next consonant
explanations.body: When ㅎ is followed or preceded by ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ or ㅈ, the two consonants are pronounced as ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ or ㅊ, respectively. Say each word and repeat it several times. (The recording is not included.) The column “change” is mine, worked out from the spelling: in 받히다 the ㄷ and ㅎ first make ㅌ, and ㅌ before 이 then becomes ㅊ (see palatalization), which gives 바치다.

explanations.title: Summary
explanations.body: ㄱ with ㅎ gives ㅋ; ㄷ with ㅎ gives ㅌ; ㅂ with ㅎ gives ㅍ; ㅈ with ㅎ gives ㅊ. It does not matter whether the ㅎ comes first (좋지, 넣다) or second (각하, 입학).

exercises.prompt: What do ㅈ and ㅎ together sound like?
exercises.explanation: ㅈ with ㅎ is pronounced ㅊ: 좋지 is said 조치.

lessons.title: 57. Palatalization
lessons.subtitle: 굳이 → 구지 · 같이 → 가치 · 닫혀요 → 다쳐요

explanations.title: Tongue toward the roof of the mouth
explanations.body:
Say tree and table, and division and song. Do you notice that t in tree is pronounced differently from t in table, and that s in division is pronounced differently from s in song? That is because the t in tree and the s in division are palatalized: they are produced with the blade (or front) of the tongue drawn up more toward the roof of the mouth than in normal pronunciation. We call this palatalization.

When a syllable-final consonant ㄷ or ㅌ is followed by the vowel ㅣ or the “y” vowels, ㄷ and ㅌ are pronounced ㅈ and ㅊ, respectively. Say each word and repeat it several times. (The recording is not included.) The book prints 닫혀요 in two steps: /다텨요/ (ㄷ + ㅎ make ㅌ) and then /다쳐요/.

explanations.title: More examples (mine)
explanations.body: Words from the standard pronunciation rules. In each one the final ㄷ or ㅌ (written ㄷ, ㅌ or, in 묻히다, with the ㅎ) meets ㅣ and is said ㅈ or ㅊ.

exercises.explanation: ㄷ becomes ㅈ: 굳이 is said 구지.

exercises.prompt: What does a syllable-final ㅌ become before ㅣ or a y-vowel?
exercises.explanation: ㅌ becomes ㅊ: 같이 is said 가치.
ㄷ and ㅌ change before ㅣ or the “y” vowels.

options: Producing a sound with the front of the tongue drawn up toward the roof of the mouth
exercises.explanation: A palatalized sound is produced with the blade of the tongue drawn up toward the roof of the mouth.

exercises.explanation: The book contrasts the t in tree (palatalized) with the t in table.

lessons.title: 58. Korean vocabulary: three components
lessons.subtitle: Sino-Korean · native · loanwords

explanations.title: Three components
explanations.body: Korean vocabulary is composed of three components: Sino-Korean words (approximately 60%), native Korean words (approximately 35%) and loanwords (approximately 5%).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean words
explanations.body: Sino- means “China” or “Chinese.” Sino-Korean vocabulary refers to a set of words that originated from, or were influenced by, the Chinese literary (written traditional) language. Sino-Korean words are easy to identify in the dictionary because they are always followed by their Chinese characters. Examples of dictionary entries:

rows: a term; a session; a semester

explanations.title: Learn the building blocks
explanations.body: Although you are not required to learn Chinese characters in the Korean Basic Course, it is important to know the meanings of the individual Sino-Korean components, because they serve as building blocks for numerous Sino-Korean words. Take the character 學 (학): it means learning or school, and is part of the following words, which all have to do with learning or school.

explanations.title: Native Korean words
explanations.body: Native Korean words are the underlying words of everyday language: food, clothing, shelter, locations, basic actions, activities and states, lower-level numerals, anatomy, natural objects, animals and so on. Thousands of sound-symbolic (onomatopoeic and mimetic) words, idioms, proverbs, and most of the grammatical markers and affixes are native Korean words. They are also easy to identify in the dictionary, because they are not followed by Chinese characters. Examples of dictionary entries (the book adds short Korean notes in brackets, [환상] for 꿈 and [꿈 같은 상태] for 꿈결, meaning “illusion” and “a dream-like state”):

rows: a dream; a vision; an illusion
a dream-like state; a dreamy (ecstatic) state of mind

explanations.title: English loanwords
explanations.body: There are over 20,000 loanwords in Korean and, fortunately, most of them (approximately 90%) are from English. Examples of English loanwords in the dictionary:

Only the first (강 江, SK) is done for you; the rest of the key is mine. A note (mine): 책 is printed without Chinese characters in the book’s table, but it is in fact Sino-Korean (冊).

lessons.title: 59. Two types of verbs
lessons.subtitle: 가다 · 먹다 · 좋다 · 슬프다 · action and stative

explanations.title: Verbs in dictionary form
explanations.body: Verbs are not only one of the key sentence elements but also, arguably, the most crucial part of speech in mastering Korean. Verbs found in the dictionary always end in 다, as in 가다 (to go; to proceed) and 먹다 (to eat). They are called “verbs in dictionary form.” Much like infinitives in English, Korean verbs are conjugated for use in a given sentence. (You learn to conjugate them in the chapters that follow this unit.)

explanations.title: Action verbs and stative verbs
explanations.body: There are two major types of verbs in Korean: action verbs and stative verbs (also known as descriptive verbs). Action verbs are those typically treated as verbs in English, and stative verbs are typically treated as adjectives in English.

rows: to be tall; to be big
tables.title: Stative verbs (SV)

explanations.title: Why the difference matters
explanations.body: Stative verbs are like English adjectives in meaning, except that they are translated as “to be …”. The distinction between the two types is crucial for your mastery of Korean, because stative verbs behave slightly differently from action verbs when they are conjugated. It is also important to keep in mind that stative verbs are not true adjectives: they cannot be placed before a modified noun unless they go through some “cosmetic changes.” In other words, to use them like English adjectives, we have to turn them into “attributive forms.” You learn how to make attributive forms later in the course.

explanations.body: The book asks you to write AV for action verbs and SV for stative verbs; the first one, 마시다, is done for you (AV). The rest of the key is mine. (Exercise 3, in which you look up ten verbs in a Korean–English dictionary, is not included. Its example row is 가다, “to go; to proceed”, AV.)

to be pretty; to be beautiful

explanations.title: What Chapter 1 teaches (인사와 소개)
explanations.body:
Chapter 1, “Greetings and Introductions”, has three topic presentations (A, B and C), five grammar points, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: exchange greetings and courtesies; introduce yourself (name, occupation, military rank); introduce others properly; ask others for biographical information; and give biographical information about yourself.

You will also become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the dictionary form of Korean verbs and the verb stem; the formal speech style verb ending 습니다 / ㅂ니다; the subject marker 이 / 가; the topic marker 은 / 는; the “linking” verb ~이다 and its negation ~이 / 가 아니다; and the Sino-Korean syllables 군 (軍) and 병 (兵).

The slash ( / ) in the book simply reads “or”. In the vocabulary lists ↑ marks an honorific form, ↓ a humble form, ~ stands for a noun or pronoun, and – for a verb stem.

explanations.title: Vocabulary strategy: sort words by theme
explanations.body: The book’s Vocabulary Builder opens with a strategy: classify the words you learn by thematic category. Classifying words by meaning and topic is an effective way of learning vocabulary. Its example sorts six words into two groups. (The chapter’s picture vocabulary presentation, three SMART Board activities and a memory game are left out.)

explanations.title: Cultural notes: how Koreans address each other
explanations.body:
Koreans often address other people with the courtesy title 선생님. Its original meaning is “teacher” or “master”, but it is also used for sir, ma’am, Mr. or Ms. The title can be preceded by the person’s last name (김 선생님).

Between close co-workers, people often address each other by first name followed by 씨 (유진 씨, 영수 씨).

Between close friends, Koreans usually address each other by first name followed by the vocative suffix 아 or 야. A first name that ends in a consonant takes 아 (유진아, 형택아); a name that ends in a vowel takes 야 (주희야, 태호야).

explanations.title: Pronunciation guide: ㅂ before ㄴ
explanations.body:
Note the spelling of these words while listening to their pronunciation. In -습니다 the ㅂ sounds like ㅁ: -습니다 becomes -슴니다, -입니다 becomes -임니다, -합니다 becomes -함니다. ㅂ changes to ㅁ whenever it is immediately followed by the nasal sound ㄴ. This is called nasalization, because ㅂ turns into ㅁ, a nasal sound, under the influence of ㄴ. You will find the same change in every verb that takes the formal ending -습니다 / ㅂ니다.

The book prints only this one change. In full speech other rules also apply, and the table below (from the pronunciation engine) shows the whole sound: for example the ㅅ after the ㅂ of 반갑 is tensed, and the ㄴ of 간 moves onto the next syllable in 오래간만입니다.

explanations.title: Notes: ~이/가 어떻게 되십니까?
explanations.body: ~이/가 어떻게 되십니까? is a very useful expression. It literally means “How does ~ become?”, but you can use it to ask for information such as a name, a person’s age, telephone number, rank, address or occupation. For example: 성함이 어떻게 되십니까?

explanations.title: Listening strategy
explanations.body: Throughout the course you will often meet situations in which you do not know every word, especially in listening practice. That is not unusual when learning a language. A good strategy is to take some risks, focus on the key words you do know, and let the unknown words pass by. These key words will most likely give you the context for what you hear and let you get the general idea. Your ability to focus on what you know and to “listen on” is a powerful learning strategy that will take you far in learning Korean. (The listening activities themselves are audio and are left out.)

lessons.title: 62. Ch 1 · Grammar A: topic markers 은 and 는
lessons.subtitle: 이름은 · 몬트레이는 · 제 고향은 뉴욕입니다

explanations.title: Topic markers 은 / 는
explanations.body:
은 and 는 are topic markers. They mark the word (or phrase) before them as the topic of the sentence, and they can be translated “as for” or “speaking of”. 은 is added to a noun that ends in a consonant (이름 → 이름은); 는 is added to a noun that ends in a vowel (몬트레이 → 몬트레이는).

In 제 이름은 이유진입니다 the literal translation is “As for my name, [it] is Lee Yujin”, which in standard English is “My name is Lee Yujin.” In 몬트레이는 제 고향입니다 it is “As for Monterey, [it] is my hometown”, i.e. “Monterey is my hometown.”

Note that 제 이름 and 몬트레이 are the topics of their sentences and that the topics happen to function as the subjects as well: a topic can overlap with the subject of a sentence (it can overlap with other functions too, but those come later). For now, knowing the basic meaning of the topic marker, choosing the right marker (은 or 는) and using it as the subject is all that is required.

lessons.title: 63. Ch 1 · Grammar B: the dictionary form and the verb stem
lessons.subtitle: 가다 · 마시다 · 먹다 · stem + 다

explanations.title: Verbs in the dictionary form
explanations.body:
Flip through a few pages of a Korean dictionary and you will find that all verbs end in 다, as in 가다 (to go; to proceed), 마시다 (to drink) and 먹다 (to eat). For that reason these are called verbs “in the dictionary form”.

The dictionary form of a Korean verb consists of a stem and the verb ending 다. When you drop 다 you get the stem: 가, 마시 and 먹 are the stems of 가다, 마시다 and 먹다. Much like English infinitives, verbs in the dictionary form have to be conjugated for use in a sentence. With few exceptions, conjugating a Korean verb means changing the ending, not the stem that carries the core meaning. So when you meet a conjugated verb whose meaning you do not know, you can look it up in a dictionary as long as you know the stem.

(The conjugation of some irregular verbs does change the stem; you will learn those in a later chapter.)

explanations.title: Speech styles and the formal style
explanations.body:
Korean has several styles of speech, each marked by its own verb ending(s). Each style conveys a different degree of politeness or formality between the speakers (or writers), so choosing the right style shows the etiquette a situation requires.

The style you see most often in this chapter is the formal style, also called formal polite speech or formal-high speech. It is marked by the verb ending 습니다 / ㅂ니다 attached to the stem. It is perceived as formal and polite because it is often used for formal purposes such as radio and television news reports. It is also used often by men, particularly when addressing superiors or making new acquaintances.

explanations.title: Subject marker or topic marker?
explanations.body:
The noun phrases 제 고향 and 제 친구 are the subjects of the sentences above. How does 이/가 differ from the topic marker 은/는, which can also function as the subject? The topic marker marks the topic of the sentence and can be translated “as for” or “speaking of”: 내 친구는 학생입니다 (“As for my friend, [he] is a student”). So the topic marker tends to be used when the speaker brings new information about the topic for the audience; the subject marker tends to be used when the subject itself is the new information.

For example, when someone asks you “Who is a DLI student?” you will probably answer 내 친구가 학생입니다 (My friend is a student), not 내 친구는 학생입니다, because 내 친구 is the new information the inquirer is seeking.

explanations.title: “Linking” verbs
explanations.body: In the English sentence “Susie is a housewife” the verb is is called a linking verb because it links the subject Susie to the noun a housewife. In Korean the verb 이다 (to be) is a linking verb, and it comes immediately after a noun, as in 나는 학생입니다 (I am a student). Its negation is ~이/가 아니다, as in 나는 학생이 아닙니다 (I am not a student).

explanations.title: What Chapter 2 teaches (우리 가족)
explanations.body:
Chapter 2, “My Family”, has three topic presentations, four grammar points, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to talk about family members using Korean kinship terms, and ask for and give biographical information such as age, jobs and marital status.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; native Korean numerals and counters; the verbs expressing possession, 있다 (to have) and 없다 (not to have); honorifics; the informal speech style verb ending 아요/어요; the conjunctive ending –고; and the Sino-Korean syllables 남 (男) and 여 (女).

explanations.title: Vocabulary strategy: flashcards for words without patterns
explanations.body:
In Chapter 1 you learned that sorting words into thematic categories is a good way to learn vocabulary. Flashcards are an effective strategy for words that do not have specific patterns. The book’s sample card has 언니 on the front and, on the back, a sentence with the word and its English meaning:

Front: 언니 · Back: 저희 언니는 서울에 살아요. / sister

Tips: first identify the vocabulary with and without patterns and sort it accordingly; make flashcards for the words without a pattern; write the Korean word large on one side, and on the other side add information that helps you understand the word in context, for example a sentence containing the word and its English meaning in small letters in the corner; and use the words in sentences as much as possible to internalize them. Flashcards are portable; when you know a card well you can move it to a “learned” pile and start on new ones, and you can go back to review. They can also be used with friends to drill in pairs or groups. (The picture/sound vocabulary presentation, the SMART Board activities, making your own flashcard and the bingo game are left out.)

explanations.title: Who calls whom: older brother and older sister
explanations.body: Korean has different words for an older sibling depending on the speaker: a male speaker says 형 (older brother) and 누나 (older sister); a female speaker says 오빠 (older brother) and 언니 (older sister). Younger siblings are 남동생 (younger brother) and 여동생 (younger sister) for either speaker. The honorific forms are 형님 and 누님.

explanations.title: Counters: noun + number + counter
explanations.body:
In Korean you count people and things in this order: noun + number + counter, as in 형 한 명. The noun can be left out if the context makes it clear. For people the counters are 명 and, for honorific use, 분 ↑.

Below is the book’s table of native Korean numbers 1 to 10. The first four change their form when a noun or counter follows: 한, 두, 세, 네.

explanations.title: Ages as the book writes them
explanations.body: Later in the chapter ages are said with the native numbers and the counter 살. These are the ages that appear in the chapter’s dialogs, activities and example sentences, so you can see how the numbers beyond 10 are built: a ten plus a one (열 + 넷 = 열네 before 살).

explanations.title: Cultural note: 우리 and 저희
explanations.body: 우리 and 저희 (a low or humble form of 우리) mean “we” or “our”, and 나 and 저 (a low form of 나) mean “I” or “me”. However, Koreans tend to use 우리 to mean “I” or “my”, as in 우리 집 (my home), 우리 학교 (my school) and 우리 회사 (my company). Some Koreans even refer to their wives as 우리 아내 (my wife) and their husbands as 우리 남편 (my husband). This follows a Korean tradition of valuing conformity to a group (such as the family or the country) over individualism.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 남 (男)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means “man”, “boy” or “male”. The book asks you to guess the meaning of three words; the book leaves the answers blank, so the meanings are mine.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 녀 / 여 (女)

explanations.title: Pronunciation guide: 몇 명 and 몇 살
explanations.body:
You know that the syllable-final consonant ㅊ sounds like ㄷ, as in 몇. Listen to the pronunciation of 몇 in 몇 명 and 몇 살: 몇 명 is said /면 명/ and 몇 살 is said /멷 쌀/ or /며 쌀/.

1. 몇 명: /멷 명/ → /면 명/. The syllable-final consonant ㄷ changes into the nasal sound ㄴ because it is assimilated by the nasal sound (ㄴ or ㅁ) that follows it. Further examples: 뒷문, 있나요, 끝나요.

2. 몇 살: /멷 살/ → /멷 쌀/ or /며 쌀/. The syllable-initial consonant (ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅈ) becomes ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ or ㅉ when it follows ㄱ, ㄷ or ㅂ, because the following sound is reinforced by the preceding one. Further examples: 학생, 있다, 학교.

explanations.title: Cultural notes: age
explanations.body:
1. Korean has two counters for age: 살 and 세 (世). 살 goes with native Korean numbers, as in 열다섯 살, and 세 goes with Sino-Korean numbers, as in 십오 세. 살 is usually used in daily conversation, while 세 is mostly used in writing, such as documents, newspapers and announcements. 살 is also often left out, as in 저는 스물다섯입니다.

2. Koreans have two ways of counting age: 만 나이 (official age) and 한국 나이 (traditional Korean age). 만 나이 starts counting from the birth of a baby, while 한국 나이 starts counting from conception, adding about a year to the person’s age. So if you are 19 years old you can be 19 or 20, depending on which 나이 you use. To say your age in 만 나이 you can say 나는 만으로 19살입니다.

explanations.title: Expressing possession
explanations.body: English uses the verb “have” to express possession (“I have an iPod”, “I don’t have a brother”). Korean says it differently:

examples.translation: naneun aipadeuga isseoyo. — I have an iPod. (literally: As for me, an iPod exists.)
naneun aipadeuga eopseoyo. — I don’t have an iPod. (literally: As for me, an iPod doesn’t exist.)

explanations.title: The pattern
explanations.body: 나는 아이파드가 있어요 literally means “As for me, an iPod exists” or “As for me, there is an iPod”; 나는 아이파드가 없어요 means “As for me, an iPod doesn’t exist” or “there isn’t an iPod”. This may sound strange to an English speaker, but it is how Koreans express possession. Keep in mind that Koreans say “there is ~” and “there isn’t ~”, so the thing you possess takes the subject marker 이/가.

lessons.title: 73. Ch 2 · Grammar B: honorifics
lessons.subtitle: 연세 · 성함 · 님 · 계시다 · 드시다 · -(으)시-

explanations.title: Four ways to express honorifics
explanations.body:
In Korean, when you talk about a person who is superior in status, you use honorifics to show the superiority of the subject. Honorifics can be expressed in four ways:

1. A few special nouns in place of regular nouns, for example 연세 instead of 나이 for “age” and 성함 instead of 이름 for “name”.
2. The honorific suffix 님 attached to a noun or title, for example 선생님, 병장님.
3. A few special verbs in place of regular verbs, for example 계시다 instead of 있다 and 드시다 instead of 먹다 for “to eat”.
4. The honorific infix –(으)시 attached to a verb, for example 이시다, 되시다, 안녕하시다.

The special nouns and special verbs are all listed in the dictionary, because they are completely different from their regular counterparts; the book’s glossary marks them with the upward arrow ↑.

rows: not to exist; not to possess
tables.title: Special nouns, the suffix 님 and special verbs

explanations.title: The honorific infix –(으)시
explanations.body: The infix –(으)시 goes between the verb stem and the verb ending: verb stem + (으)시 + verb ending. After a stem that ends in a consonant it is 으시; after a stem that ends in a vowel it is 시. With the formal ending ㅂ니다 the ㅂ attaches to 시, so 일하 + 시 + ㅂ니다 is said 일하십니다.

rows: The stem ends in a consonant
읽다 → 읽 + 으시 + ㅂ니다; 많다 → 많 + 으시 + ㅂ니다
The stem ends in a vowel
이다 → 이 + 시 + ㅂ니다; 일하다 → 일하 + 시 + ㅂ니다

lessons.title: 75. Ch 2 · Grammar C: the informal speech style -아요 / -어요
lessons.subtitle: 좋아요 · 있어요 · 가요 · 와요 · 해요 · 이에요 / 예요 · -(으)세요

explanations.title: The informal polite style
explanations.body: The informal speech style, marked by the verb ending –아/어요, is the most widely used in spoken Korean. It is used when the speaker (or writer) is in a casual yet polite relationship with the person addressed, so it is also called informal polite speech or informal-high speech. Unlike the formal ending –ㅂ/습니다 from Chapter 1, you can use –아/어요 for a statement, a question, a command or request, and even a suggestion without changing its form. Intonation and context tell you which one is meant.

rows: The last syllable of the stem has the vowel ㅏ or ㅗ
The last syllable of the stem has any other vowel

examples.translation: nunaga eodieseo sarayo? — Where does your older sister live?
nunaneun seoureseo sarayo. — She lives in Seoul.
gim seonsaengnimeun dongsaengi isseoyo? — Mr. Kim, do you have any younger siblings?
jeoneun dongsaengeun eopseoyo. hyeongman isseoyo. — No, I don’t. I have only an older brother.

explanations.title: When the stem ends in a vowel: deletion and contraction
explanations.body:
When 아/어요 is added to a stem that ends in a vowel (가 in 가다), a deletion or contraction occurs:

• stem ends in ㅏ or ㅓ: the 아 or 어 is deleted (가 + 아요 → 가요; 서 + 어요 → 서요).
• stem ends in ㅡ and is one syllable: the ㅡ is deleted and –어요 is attached (크 + 어요 → 커요).
• stem ends in ㅡ and has more than one syllable: the ㅡ is deleted and –아요 or –어요 is attached, depending on the vowel before ㅡ (바쁘 + 아요 → 바빠요; 슬프 + 어요 → 슬퍼요).
• contraction: 오 + 아요 → 와요 (ㅗ + ㅏ = ㅘ); 다니 + 어요 → 다녀요 (ㅣ + ㅓ = ㅕ).
• 하다 is the only verb with a stem in ㅏ that behaves differently: 하 + 아요 → 해요; 공부하 + 아요 → 공부해요; 일하다 → 일해요.

explanations.title: ~이다 and the honorific infix
explanations.body:
~이다 is the only verb that behaves this way: after a noun that ends in a consonant it is 이에요; after a noun that ends in a vowel 이에요 can contract to 예요 (학생이다 → 학생이에요; 의사이다 → 의사예요).

When you add the honorific infix –(으)시 (page “Honorifics”), 어요 has to follow, and (으)시어요 contracts to (으)세요: 계시 + 어요 → 계세요; 하시 + 어요 → 하세요.

lessons.title: 76. Ch 2 · Grammar D: connecting clauses with -고
lessons.subtitle: 저는 군인이고 친구는 학생입니다 · stem + 고

explanations.title: The conjunctive ending -고
explanations.body:
In English, when we connect two or more clauses we use connecting words (conjunctions) such as and, or, because, when, before. In Korean, we use verb endings attached to the stem of a verb, called conjunctive or connective endings. Throughout the course you will learn quite a few of them, and the very first is –고, which means “and”.

In 저는 군인이고 친구는 학생입니다, 고 is attached to the stem of the verb 이다 in the first clause, so the whole sentence is “I am a serviceman and my friend is a student.”

If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with so they can offer other activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

explanations.title: What Chapter 3 teaches (우리 집)
explanations.body:
Chapter 3, “My House”, has three topic presentations, four grammar points (the book’s Topic C has its own two: the object marker and ~에서), activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: talk about the layout of a house; talk about the location of objects in relation to each other; describe objects using size and colors; and talk about typical daily activities in specific locations.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the verbs that express existence, ~에 있다 and ~에 없다; the demonstratives 이, 그 and 저; the object marker ~을/를; the location marker that works with action verbs, ~에서; and the Sino-Korean syllables 색 (色), 식 (食) and 실 (室).

explanations.title: Vocabulary strategy: understand the “verb maker” ~하다
explanations.body:
Korean has borrowed a large number of Chinese words as well as words from other languages, and many have become an integral part of the vocabulary. Most of these borrowed words are nouns and cannot be used as verbs as they are. To use them as verbs we add 하다. 하다, literally “to do”, readily turns borrowed words into verbs. For example, 식사 (食事) is a Sino-Korean word meaning “meal” or “eating”; adding 하다 gives the verb 식사하다, “to eat” or “to dine”. Another example is the borrowed English word 골프 (golf): adding 하다 turns it into a verb phrase meaning “to play golf”.

The book gives six Sino-Korean nouns and nine English loan words and asks you to make them into verbs and guess the meanings; the verbs and meanings below are my key.

explanations.title: 하다 with pure Korean words, and the object marker
explanations.body: The “verb maker” 하다 also works well with many pure Korean words (설거지하다, 일하다, 밥하다). When 하다 turns a noun into an action verb, as in 공부하다 (to study) and 이메일하다 (to email), the object marker ~을/를 can be inserted between the noun and 하다. In spoken language, however, the object marker is usually left out. Both of these are correct:

lessons.title: 81. Ch 3 · Grammar A: ~에 있다 and ~에 없다 (existence at a place)
lessons.subtitle: 제 동생이 뉴욕에 있어요 · 계세요 · 학교가 몬트레이에 있어요

explanations.title: Verbs that express existence
explanations.body:
In Chapter 2 you learned that Koreans use 있다 and 없다 to express possession, as in 나는 아이파드가 있어요 (I have an iPod). The literal meanings are “As for me, an iPod exists” and “doesn’t exist”, because the verbs literally mean “to exist” and “not to exist”. So Koreans also use these verbs to say that an object or a person is or is not at a certain place. The location marker ~에 (in 기숙사에, 뉴욕에) can be translated “at”, “on” or “in”.

When you speak of the location of a person of higher status, such as your teacher, commander, parents or grandparents, use 계시다 ↑ and 안 계시다 ↑ instead of 있다 and 없다.

tables.title: The pattern (~에 있다 / ~에 없다; ~에 계시다 ↑ / ~에 안 계시다 ↑)

je aipadeuga gisuksae eopseoyo. — My iPod is not in the dormitory.
je dongsaengi nyuyoge isseoyo. — My younger brother is in New York.
je dongsaengi nyuyoge eopseoyo. — My younger brother is not in New York.

explanations.title: Word order and nuance
explanations.body:
In Korean it is easy to tell how nouns are used because they are followed by markers (subject, object, topic, location). In 우리 학교가 몬트레이에 있어요 you can tell the functions of 우리 학교 and 몬트레이 from the subject marker 가 and the location marker 에, so you can re-position the two nouns without changing the meaning: 우리 학교가 몬트레이에 있어요 / 몬트레이에 우리 학교가 있어요 (My school is in Monterey).

Occasionally, re-positioning the subject and the location changes the nuance: 학교가 몬트레이에 있어요 means “The school is in Monterey”, but 몬트레이에 학교가 있어요 means “There is a school in Monterey”. When an unspecified noun such as 학교 (school), 사람 (people) or 초콜렛 (chocolate) is the subject in the first configuration, it is read as “the ~”; when it comes after the location, as in the second, it is read as “a ~”.

monteureie uri hakgyoga isseoyo. — My school is in Monterey.
hakgyoga monteureie isseoyo. — The school is in Monterey.
monteureie hakgyoga isseoyo. — There is a school in Monterey.

lessons.title: 82. Ch 3 · Grammar B: the demonstratives 이, 그 and 저
lessons.subtitle: 이 책상 · 그 책상 · 저 책상 · 이것 · 그것 · 저것 · 이건 · 이게

explanations.title: Three demonstratives
explanations.body:
Demonstratives are the words used to point to an object or a person in sight, as in “this book/man” or “that book/man over there”. Korean has three: 이, 그 and 저.

이 refers to an object or person near the speaker; 그 refers to an object or person near the listener but away from the speaker; 저 refers to an object or person away from both the speaker and the listener. 그 can also refer to something or someone out of sight which both the speaker and the listener know about, or which has been mentioned before.

rows: Near the listener, away from the speaker
Away from both the speaker and the listener

explanations.title: How they are used
explanations.body: English demonstratives can be pronouns (“I bought these”), adjectives (“I wore that dress”) or even adverbs (“The fish was this big”). Korean demonstratives are used mainly as adjectives that modify nouns, so 이, 그 and 저 are usually followed by the noun being modified (이 책, 저 선생님, 그 컴퓨터). Used alone as “this thing”, the forms are 이것 (이거), 그것 (그거) and 저것 (저거). 것 is often shortened to 거 in informal speech; there is no space between the demonstrative and 것/거.

explanations.title: Contracted forms
explanations.body: With the markers 은 and 이, 이것 / 그것 / 저것 have contracted forms.

lessons.title: 85. Ch 3 · Grammar D: the location marker ~에서 with action verbs
lessons.subtitle: 도서관에 있어요 · 도서관에서 공부해요 · 방에서 음악을 들어요

explanations.title: ~에 or ~에서?
explanations.body:
Recall that the location marker 에 is used with 있다 or 없다 and is translated “at”, “on” or “in”. There is one more location marker with the same meaning: 에서. While ~에 is used with 있다, 없다 and 계시다 (the honorific form of 있다), ~에서 is for action verbs.

In 저는 도서관에 있어요 (I am in the library) 에 goes with 있어요; in 저는 도서관에서 공부해요 (I study in the library) 에서 goes with 공부해요, which is an action verb.

units.title: Semester 1 · Unit 1 · Chapter 4: My Life at DLI (DLI 생활)

lessons.title: 88. Ch 4 · Topic A: Facilities, countries and languages
lessons.subtitle: 저희 학교를 소개하겠습니다 · 도서관 · 우체국 · 기숙사 · 한국어 · 관 · 장 · 국 · 어 · 인

explanations.title: What Chapter 4 teaches (DLI 생활)
explanations.body:
Chapter 4, “My Life at DLI”, has three topic presentations, four grammar points, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: describe the locations of the DLI facilities using spatial terms; comprehend and respond to simple classroom instructions; and ask for and give directions.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the polite request/command forms -(으)세요 and -지 마세요; ㄹ irregular verbs; the direction/destination marker (으)로 (toward; to); the attributive form of a stative verb -(으)ㄴ; and the Sino-Korean syllables 관 (館), 장 (場), 국 (國), 어 (語) and 인 (人).

explanations.title: Vocabulary strategy: use the words you already know
explanations.body:
In the past three chapters you have acquired quite a few words and a few strategies. Use the words you already know as a point of reference instead of rote memorization. The book gives three examples:

1. 식당 “a restaurant; a cafeteria”. You learned the Sino-Korean 식 (食), eating, meal, food, in Chapter 3, and words that contain it, such as 식사하다 (to have a meal) and 음식 (food). Since 식당 is a place for having a meal, you can figure out the meaning of 당 and easily recall 식당.
2. 교실 “a classroom”. Recall 실 (室), a room, as in 침실 and 거실. You have not learned the Sino-Korean 교 yet, but you have seen it in 학교 (a school). So it is easier to construct and remember the meaning of 교실.
3. 사거리 “an intersection; a crossroads”. 사 (four) is one of the numbers you learned in Chapter 2. An intersection is a point where two streets cross, forming a four-way junction, so you can guess that 거리 is a way, street or road. Since you know what 사 and 거리 mean, you can tell what 삼거리 and 오거리 mean.

Language is a system in which the same patterns occur repeatedly.

explanations.title: 어 (語) and 말
explanations.body:
1. Both 어 (語) and 말 refer to a language or a word. 어 is a Sino-Korean word and must be used as part of another word, as in 한국어 and 중국어. In contrast, the pure Korean word 말 can stand alone. 어 is usually “language” or “word”; 말 can be language, word, speech, utterance or talk, depending on the context.
2. ~말 can be interchangeable with ~어, as in 일본어 / 일본말, 중국어 / 중국말, 한국어 / 한국말.
3. When 어 is preceded by a Sino-Korean country name such as 일본어, 중국어, 불란서어 and 러시아어, often the rest of the syllables of the country name (except the first syllable) are dropped: 독(일)어 → 독어, 일(본)어 → 일어, 불(란서)어 → 불어. Note that ~말 is not interchangeable with ~어 in shortened forms.
