explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable is made up of 食 (식), meaning meal or food, and 官 (관), meaning a government post. It originally meant a government post for military people to stay at (or to eat). It has developed to mean an (official) building, a house, an inn, a store or a restaurant. explanations.title: Pronunciation guide: a final consonant before a vowel
explanations.body:
In English, “stop it” and “bull’s eye” are pronounced /staa pit/ and /bul zai/, as if they were spelled “sto pit” and “bull seye”. We can observe this phenomenon in Korean as well.

1. When a syllable-final consonant is followed by a vowel, the sound of the final consonant is carried over to the next syllable.
2. When a consonant cluster is followed by a vowel, only the second consonant is carried over to the next vowel.

explanations.title: Making polite requests and commands
explanations.body: In English, when we make a polite request, we use “please”, as in “Please go home” or “Please don’t go home”. In Korean we make a polite request by adding -(으)세요 or -지 마세요 to the verb stem of an action verb.

The verb stem ends in a vowel

rows: The verb stem ends in a consonant or a vowel
앉다 → 앉지 마세요; 펴다 → 펴지 마세요

explanations.title: -(으)세요 is also a statement and a question
explanations.body: Keep in mind that -(으)세요 is a combination of the honorific marker 시 and the informal speech style ending 어요. Like -어요, -(으)세요 can be a statement, a question or a polite request depending on the context and intonation. (The book writes “TV”; here it is written 티브이 so that it can be spoken.)

lessons.title: 91. Ch 4 · Grammar B: ㄹ irregular verbs
lessons.subtitle: 열다 → 엽니다 · 살다 → 삽니다 · 알다 → 아세요 · 졸다 · 돌다 · 멀다 · 떠들다

explanations.title: Verbs whose stems end in ㄹ
explanations.body:
The Korean language has quite a few verbs whose stems end in ㄹ: 열다 (to open), 살다 (to live), 알다 (to know), 졸다 (to doze) and others. These are known as ㄹ irregular verbs because they drop the ㄹ when their stems are followed by ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ. (It is easy to remember these consonants as NPS: N for ㄴ, P for ㅂ, S for ㅅ.)

There are four common situations when the stems are followed by ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ:
1. -ㅂ니다 (formal polite ending): 엽니다, 삽니다, 압니다, 좁니다.
2. -십니다 (the honorific 시 + ㅂ니다): 여십니다, 사십니다, 아십니다, 조십니다.
3. -세요 (the honorific 시 + 어요): 여세요, 사세요, 아세요, 조세요.
4. -는 (the attributive form of the verb): 문을 여는 학생 (a student who opens the door), 뉴욕에 사는 학생 (a student who lives in New York). The book deals with this fourth situation later.

rows: The verb stem ends in ㄹ and is followed by ㄴ, ㅂ or ㅅ
열다: 여 + ㅂ니다 → 엽니다; 여 + 십니다 → 여십니다
살다: 사 + ㅂ니다 → 삽니다; 사 + 십니다 → 사십니다

i seonsaengnim, geu apateu aseyo? — Do you know that apartment, Mr. Lee?
je dongsaengi nyuyoge samnida. — My younger brother lives in New York.

explanations.title: Direction / destination marker: noun + (으)로

lessons.subtitle: 큰 집 · 좋은 집 · 빨간 사과 · 하얀 건물 · 먼 나라 · 넓은 주차장

explanations.title: Stative verbs before a noun
explanations.body:
Recall the Korean “adjectives” you learned in Chapter 2: 넓다 (to be wide), 많다 (to be many/much), 아름답다 (to be beautiful) and others. In English they are adjectives, but in Korean they are verbs. Their dictionary forms all end in -다 (크다, 예쁘다, 넓다) and they can be conjugated (많습니다, 많아요, 많고, 많아서). Because of these verb-like characteristics they are called stative verbs or descriptive verbs.

Unlike English adjectives, which can modify a noun freely as in “a beautiful house” or “a large boat”, Korean stative verbs cannot modify a noun unless they go through some “cosmetic” changes and are turned into the attributive form: stative verb stem + (으)ㄴ + noun.

rows: The verb stem ends in a vowel
The verb stem ends in a consonant

explanations.title: Color verbs
explanations.body: For stative verbs for colors, drop ㅎ and add ㄴ to the stem, as if the stem ended in a vowel: 빨갛다 → 빨갛 → (drop ㅎ) 빨가 + ㄴ → 빨간 (red). (The English is the book’s.)

explanations.title: A note on 멀다 → 먼 (my remark)

The book does not state this rule for the attributive form; the remark is mine. 가깝다 (near) turns into 가까운 (a ㅂ-changing verb that the book has not explained yet); the form is given for reference.

explanations.title: Activity 1 (classroom): the commands left out in part; Simon Says
explanations.body: The listening part (matching five classroom conversations to pictures) and the picture part (writing the proper command under each of five pictures) depend on audio and pictures. In Activity 2 you write three commands in Korean on cards and play “Simon Says”, which in Korean is 대장님 가라사대 (literally, “the chief says”). Simon reads a command with or without 대장님 가라사대 in front of it; the class obeys only a command preceded by it. For example, if Simon says 대장님 가라사대, “앉으세요”, everyone must sit down; if Simon simply says “앉으세요”, no one should move.

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body: The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences are the book’s; the book gives no English for them). Where the book prints two forms together (건너편/맞은편, 불어/프랑스어, 조금/좀, 곧장/쭉, 첫 번째/첫째) each is shown on its own row, and where it writes 우회전(하다) the verb is shown. Some examples contain letters or numerals in the book (DLI, PFC, LA, “65쪽”, “7시”); here they are written in Hangul (디엘아이, 피에프씨, 엘에이, 육십오 쪽, 일곱 시) so they can be spoken. I have also written 체육관 / 쪽 / 남쪽 without a leading “~”, and the markers 에서 and (으)로 as rows 에서, 으로, 로; the attributive ending -(으)ㄴ (“attributive form for stative verbs”) is explained in Grammar D. Four example sentences that the book prints once for two forms of a word (프랑스어, 맞은편, 넷째 … and 좀) are my adaptations of the book’s sentences.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with so they can offer other activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: describe the locations of the DLI facilities using spatial terms; comprehend and respond to simple classroom instructions; ask for and give directions.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the polite request/command forms -(으)세요 and -지 마세요; ㄹ irregular verbs; the direction/destination marker (으)로 (toward; to); the attributive form of stative verbs -(으)ㄴ; and the Sino-Korean syllables 관 (館), 장 (場), 국 (國), 어 (語) and 인 (人).

explanations.title: What Chapter 5 teaches (하루 일과)
explanations.body:
Chapter 5, “Daily Activities”, has three topic presentations, four grammar points, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: ask and answer questions about time; talk about daily routines; and ask and answer questions about days of the week, dates, months and years.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the direction markers 에서 (from) and 에 (to); the conjunctive ending for sequential actions -아서/-어서 (and then); ~ 전에 / -기 전에 (before); ~ 후에 / -(으)ㄴ 후에 (after); the informal blunt speech style verb ending 아/어; and the Sino-Korean syllables 매 (每), 일 (日), 전 (前), 주 (週) and 후 (後).

explanations.title: Vocabulary strategy: group synonyms and antonyms
explanations.body: While learning Korean you will meet words with similar or identical meanings (synonyms) or opposite meanings (antonyms). Grouping synonyms or antonyms helps you remember them more easily. The book gives these groups of similar meaning: 우회전하다 = 오른쪽으로 돌다 and 세탁하다 = 빨래하다; and these of opposite meaning: 오전 (a.m.) ↔ 오후 (p.m.), 남 ↔ 여, 일찍 (early) ↔ 늦게 (late), 낮 (day) ↔ 밤 (night). (↔ denotes antonyms.)

explanations.title: Vocabulary Builder: match the antonyms
explanations.body: The book gives four pairs to match: 시작 (beginning), 자주 (often), 자다, 끝 (end), 열다, 가끔 (occasionally), 일어나다, 닫다. The first one is done for you (자다 ↔ 일어나다 is not it; the pairing is mine). The key is mine.

explanations.title: How to read the time in Korean
explanations.body: The hour is a pure Korean number + 시; the minutes are a Sino-Korean number + 분: 1시 45분 = 한 시 사십오 분, or 두 시 십오 분 전 (“fifteen minutes before 2”). 4시 30분 = 네 시 삼십 분, or 네 시 반 (반 = half).

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 매 (每) and 일 (日)
explanations.body: The first syllable of 매일 is 매 (每), meaning every or each, as in 매달 (every month; each month) and 매년 (every year; each year). The second syllable 일 (日) depicts the sun and so means the sun or a day, as in 일요일 (Sunday) and 평일 (weekday; “regular day”). The book warns you not to confuse this 日 (the sun; a day) with 一 (one), because they sound the same.

lessons.title: 99. Ch 5 · Grammar A: the direction markers ~에서 and ~에
lessons.subtitle: 산호세에서 와요 · 산호세에 가요 · from and to

explanations.title: 에서 and 에 with movement verbs
explanations.body:
Recall the location markers 에서 and 에 from Chapter 3. They are interpreted as “at”, “on” or “in”, as in 저는 몬트레이에서 공부해요 (I study in Monterey) and 저는 몬트레이에 있어요 (I am in Monterey).

However, when these markers are used with movement verbs such as 가다 (to go) and 오다 (to come), they are direction markers: 에서 is interpreted as “from” and 에 as “to”: 저는 산호세에서 와요 (I am coming from San Jose), 저는 산호세에 가요 (I am going to San Jose).

So ~에서 and ~에 have dual meanings that are determined strictly by the verbs that accompany them. Because Korean verbs are usually placed at the end of a sentence, listeners cannot determine the specific meaning of ~에서 and ~에 until they hear the verb.

headers: With 있다 / 없다 or an action verb

explanations.title: -고 and -아서/-어서
explanations.body:
Recall that the first conjunctive ending -고 from Chapter 2 is translated “and”. In the second sentence below, -고 implies that the two actions, eating and taking a shower, occur in sequence: “In the morning I eat and then take a shower.”

Likewise, the conjunctive ending -아서/-어서 can connect two actions or events in sequence. However, -아서/-어서 is used when the first verb shows motion, such as 가다 (to go), 오다 (to come) or 일어나다 (to get up). Other Korean verbs that show motion are 서다 (to stand up), 앉다 (to sit down), 나가다 (to go out), 나오다 (to come out) and so on.

-아서/-어서 can also connect clauses in a cause-and-effect relationship; the book discusses that in Chapter 7.

explanations.title: The rule: verb stem + -아서/어서
explanations.body: When the last syllable of the verb stem contains the vowel ㅏ or ㅗ, add 아서: 가 + 아서 → 가서; 오 + 아서 → 와서. When the last syllable contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ, add 어서: 일어서 + 어서 → 일어서서. (The forms below are mine; the examples are the book’s.)

explanations.title: “Before”: ~ 전에 and -기 전에
explanations.body: In English “before” and “after” show that an event, date or time precedes or follows another. Koreans use ~ 전에 or -기 전에 for “before” and ~ 후에 or -(으)ㄴ 후에 for “after”. ~ 전에 and ~ 후에 follow a noun denoting an event, date or time, as in 수업 전에 (before class); -기 전에 and -(으)ㄴ 후에 follow the stem of a verb denoting an activity, as in 학교 가기 전에 (before going to school) or 먹은 후에 (after eating).

rows: 식사 → 식사 전에; 수업 → 수업 전에
먹다 → 먹기 전에; 식사하다 → 식사하기 전에
tables.title: “Before”: noun + 전에; verb stem + 기 전에

examples.translation: sueop jeone cheyukgwaneseo undonghaeyo. — Before class, I work out at the gym.

explanations.title: “After”: ~ 후에 and -(으)ㄴ 후에
explanations.body: After a noun add 후에 (수업 → 수업 후에). When a verb stem ends in a consonant add 은 후에 (먹다 → 먹은 후에); when it ends in a vowel add ㄴ 후에 (공부하다 → 공부한 후에). The book’s footnote adds that you can also say “after -ing” with (으)ㄴ 다음에, as in 공부한 다음에 비디오 게임을 합니다.

A verb stem ending in a vowel

lessons.title: 103. Ch 5 · Grammar D: the informal blunt style (반말)
lessons.subtitle: 많아 · 있어 · 먹어 · 이야 · 야 · 아니야 · 먹지 마

explanations.title: Informal polite → informal blunt
explanations.body: Recall the informal speech style -아요/어요 from Chapter 2. It is used in casual yet polite settings where social distance needs to be maintained. Removing 요 from -아요/어요 gives the informal blunt speech style, which is typically used where social distance does not need to be maintained (between friends or siblings). Older people also use it with younger people they are close to. (It is also known as the informal plain form, the informal non-polite form and the intimate form; in Korean, 반말.)

explanations.body: ~이에요/~예요 → ~이야/~야; 아니에요 → 아니야; -지 마세요 → -지 마. (The book’s ~야 is for nouns that end in a vowel, ~이야 for those that end in a consonant.)

explanations.title: What Chapter 6 teaches (날씨와 취미)
explanations.body:
Chapter 6, “Weather and Hobbies”, has three topic presentations, four grammar points, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: talk about the four seasons and the weather; and talk about hobbies and weekend activities in a simple phrase or sentence.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; -고 싶다 / 싶어하다 (want to; wish to); -(으)러 가다 / 오다 (go/come to do something); ㅂ irregular verbs; and the Sino-Korean syllable 구 (球). (The book’s “Let’s …” section, -(으)ㅂ시다, is in the chapter too.)

explanations.title: A note on 끼었습니다 (past tense for the present weather)
explanations.body: You will hear native speakers say 오늘은 안개가 끼었습니다, “it is foggy today”, or 오늘은 구름이 끼었습니다, “it is cloudy today”. Because 끼었습니다 is the past tense of 끼다, you may wonder why a Korean speaker would use the past tense to describe the present weather. 끼다 literally means “to form”. When you say 구름이 낍니다 (present tense) you are saying that clouds are forming now. When you say 구름이 끼었습니다 the sentence implies that clouds have already formed and, as a result, it is cloudy.

explanations.title: Stative verbs whose stems end in ㅂ
explanations.body: So far you have learned quite a few stative verbs whose stems end in ㅂ: 쉽다 (to be easy), 어렵다 (to be difficult), 춥다 (to be cold), 덥다 (to be hot), 가깝다 (to be close; to be near), 반갑다 (to be glad) and 고맙다 (to be thankful). These are commonly known as ㅂ irregular verbs, because when the verb stem is followed by a vowel in conjugation, the ㅂ is dropped from the stem and 우 is added.

rows: The stem ends in ㅂ and is followed by a vowel
덥 + 어요 → 더우어요 → 더워요; 쉽 + 어요 → 쉬우어요 → 쉬워요

lessons.title: 109. Ch 6 · Grammar B: expressing wishes with -고 싶다 and -고 싶어하다
lessons.subtitle: 먹고 싶어요 · 가고 싶어요 · 먹고 싶어해요 · 배우고 싶어해요

explanations.title: Want to, wish to, would like to
explanations.body: In English we use “want to”, “wish to” and “would like to”. In Korean we use -고 싶다 or -고 싶어하다. If the subject is the first person (I, we) or the second person (you), -고 싶다 is used; if the subject is the third person (he, she, John, they and so on), -고 싶어하다 is used. They attach to the stem of an action verb.

rows: The subject is 1st or 2nd person (I, we, you)
add 고 싶다 to the verb stem
먹다 → 먹고 싶다; 공부하다 → 공부하고 싶다
The subject is 3rd person (he, she, they, etc.)
add 고 싶어하다 to the verb stem
먹다 → 먹고 싶어하다; 공부하다 → 공부하고 싶어하다

explanations.title: Dialog: what do you usually do on the weekend?
explanations.body: Mike, a DLI student, and his conversation partner Soyeon, a graduate student, are talking about their weekend activities and hobbies. The book’s footnote says the -기 in 달리기 (running) is a “gerund maker” attached to a verb stem; you will learn it in a later chapter. (The English is mine.)

explanations.title: To go to do something
explanations.body: When we go to a restaurant to eat we say “I am going (to the restaurant) to eat.” “To eat” following the verb “is going” shows the purpose of going. Koreans express the purpose of coming and going with -(으)러 가다 or -(으)러 오다, as in 점심을 먹으러 (식당에) 갑니다 or 점심을 먹으러 (식당에) 옵니다.

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body: The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences are the book’s; the book gives no English for them). Where the book writes a noun with (~하다) the verb is shown on its own row, and the endings -고 싶다/-고 싶어하다, -(으)러 가다/오다 and -(으)ㅂ시다 are written without the leading hyphen and parentheses: 고 싶다, 고 싶어하다, 으러 가다, 으러 오다, 읍시다, ㅂ시다. In the examples, DLI is written 디엘아이, and four example sentences are my adaptations of the book’s (the book’s 영화가 아주 재미있어요 for 재미있다 is the book’s “007 시리즈가 아주 재미있어요”, with the digits left out; the book’s L.A. Dodgers and “빅서” sentences keep only the Korean words).

explanations.title: What Chapter 7 teaches (몬트레이 시내에서)
explanations.body:
Chapter 7, “Downtown Monterey”, has three topic presentations, four grammar points, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: list and discuss businesses around town; order food and drink at a restaurant; and ask for services at a hair salon or barber shop.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the negating adverbs 안 and 못; the conjunctive ending -아/어서 for cause and effect (and thus; because); the auxiliary verb -아/어 주다 used to express “the sense of providing service”; -(으)ㄹ까요? (Shall we …?); and the Sino-Korean syllables 소 (所), 음 (飮) and 점 (店).

explanations.title: Strategy: construct a phrase or sentence from related words
explanations.body: If you learn words in context, you are more likely to retain them longer and recognize them better. When you work on a set of new words, first group related words and then construct a phrase or sentence that uses them. For example, with the four new words 돈 (money), 기름 (gasoline), 찾다 (to withdraw) and 넣다 (to put in), group 돈 with 찾다 and 기름 with 넣다, and then build a phrase with each pair.

lessons.subtitle: 뭐 드시겠어요? · 불고기 · 비빔밥 · 만두 · 맥주 · 계산서 · 음 (飮)

explanations.title: Dialog: what would you like to eat?
explanations.body: At a Korean restaurant, PFC Thomas and his Korean friend Jinyeong are about to place an order. The book’s footnote: 뭐 드시겠어요? is a common expression used at a restaurant and means “What would you like to have?”; 뭐 is a contracted form of 무엇. (The English is mine.)

examples.translation: jongeobwon: mwo deusigesseoyo? — What would you like to have?

examples.text: 진영: 토마스 씨, 매운 음식 괜찮아요?
examples.translation: jinyeong: tomaseu ssi, maeun eumsik gwaenchanayo? — Thomas, is spicy food okay for you?

examples.text: 토마스: 저는 매운 음식은 못 먹어요. 김치도 매워서 못 먹어요.
examples.translation: tomaseu: jeoneun maeun eumsigeun mon meogeoyo. gimchido maewoseo mon meogeoyo. — I can’t eat spicy food. I can’t eat kimchi either because it is spicy.

examples.text: 진영: 그래요? 그럼, 불고기하고 비빔밥 어때요?
examples.translation: jinyeong: geuraeyo? geureom, bulgogihago bibimbap eottaeyo? — Is that so? Then how about bulgogi and bibimbap?

examples.text: 토마스: 네, 좋아요. 우리 만두도 시킵시다. 오늘은 아주 배가 고파요.
examples.translation: tomaseu: ne, joayo. uri mandudo sikipsida. oneureun aju baega gopayo. — Yes, good. Let’s order dumplings too. I am very hungry today.

examples.text: 진영: 그래요. 여기 불고기 일 인분, 만두 일 인분, 비빔밥 하나 주세요.
examples.translation: jinyeong: geuraeyo. yeogi bulgogi il inbun, mandu il inbun, bibimbap hana juseyo. — Okay. Please give us one serving of bulgogi, one serving of dumplings and one bibimbap.

examples.text: 종업원: 네, 알겠습니다. 음료수는 뭐 드시겠어요?
examples.translation: jongeobwon: ne, algetseumnida. eumnyosuneun mwo deusigesseoyo? — Yes, understood. What would you like to drink?

examples.text: 진영: 저는 콜라 한 잔 주세요.
examples.translation: jinyeong: jeoneun kolla han jan juseyo. — I would like a glass of cola, please.

examples.text: 토마스: 저는 맥주 한 병 주세요. 그리고 물도 좀 갖다 주세요.
examples.translation: tomaseu: jeoneun maekju han byeong juseyo. geurigo muldo jom gatda juseyo. — I would like a bottle of beer, please. And please bring some water too.

examples.text: 진영: 여기 계산서 좀 주세요. 신용카드 받습니까?
examples.translation: jinyeong: yeogi gyesanseo jom juseyo. sinyongkadeu batseumnikka? — (After finishing the meal) Please give us the bill. Do you accept credit cards?

explanations.title: Naming the food of a country
explanations.body: When referring to food from different countries or regions, add 음식 after a country or regional name, as in 한국음식, 미국음식, 서양음식 (Western food) and 일본음식. 한국음식 is usually abbreviated as 한식, 서양음식 as 양식, and 일본음식 as 일식.

explanations.title: Cultural note: kimchi
explanations.body: Kimchi is a traditional Korean fermented dish made of vegetables with a variety of seasonings. It is the most common side dish served with Korean meals. Although Koreans make kimchi from many vegetables, the Napa cabbage kimchi (배추 김치) is the most common type. Koreans make dishes like kimchi stew (김치찌개), kimchi fried rice (김치볶음밥) and even kimchi pizza (김치피자). Despite its spicy flavor, many foreigners in Korea develop a taste for kimchi and find themselves missing it after returning home. The dish is so essential to Koreans that “space kimchi” was developed by the Korea Aerospace Research Institute for the first Korean astronaut.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 음 (飮)
explanations.body: This Sino-Korean syllable means drink or swallow.

explanations.title: Counting drinks and dishes
explanations.body: In the dialog the customers order with the counters 병 (bottles), 잔 (glasses and cups) and 인분 (servings). The native numbers 한, 두, 세, 네 go before 병 and 잔; the Sino-Korean numbers 일, 이, 삼, 사 go before 인분 (the book’s examples are 불고기 일 인분, 맥주 한 병, 콜라 한 잔, 맥주 두 병, 불고기 사 인분하고 맥주 세 병).

explanations.title: Reading: a survey of the favorite dishes of foreigners in Korea
explanations.body: The article, in the book: “한국 음식 베스트 10: 외국인은 어떤 한국 음식을 좋아할까요? 한국 관광 공사가 외국인 1635명에게 질문했습니다. 외국인들은 비빔밥 (63.2%), 불고기 (57.8%), 갈비 (46.7%), 냉면 (39.5%), 삼계탕 (39.1%), 순두부찌개 (32.4%), 해물파전 (26.4%), 잡채 (25.4%), 김치 (25.3%), 김밥 (17.8%)을 좋아합니다.” The book glosses 한국 관광 공사 as the Korean Tourism Organization and 질문하다 as “to ask a question; to inquire”. explanations.title: Dialog: how do you want your hair cut?
explanations.body: Mr. Park is visiting a hair salon to get his hair cut. The book’s footnotes: 짧게 is the adverb of 짧다; simply by adding 게 to the stem of a stative verb we turn the verb into an adverb; 좀 is an abbreviation of 조금 (a little). (The English is mine.)

examples.text: 미용사: 어서 오세요. 몇 시 예약이세요?
examples.translation: miyongsa: eoseo oseyo. myeot si yeyagiseyo? — Welcome. What time is your reservation?
bakjinsu: ne, se si yeyagimnida. — Yes, I have a three o’clock reservation.

examples.text: 미용사: 아, 네. 손님, 저쪽으로 갈까요?
examples.translation: miyongsa: a, ne. sonnim, jeojjogeuro galkkayo? — Oh, yes. Sir, shall we go over there?
miyongsa: meori eotteoke hae deurilkkayo? — (After taking him to the chair) How would you like your hair done?

examples.text: 박진수: 짧게 자르고 싶습니다. 그런데 앞머리는 좀 길게 해 주세요.
examples.translation: bakjinsu: jjalge jareugo sipseumnida. geureonde ammeorineun jom gilge hae juseyo. — I want to cut it short. But please make the bangs a little long.

bakjinsu: a, geuraeyo? yeomsaegeun eolmayeyo? — Oh, is that so? How much is the dye?
miyongsa: yeomsaegeun palsibo dalleoyeyo. — The dye is eighty-five dollars.

examples.text: 박진수: 그럼 짙은 갈색으로 해 주세요.
examples.translation: bakjinsu: geureom jiteun galsaegeuro hae juseyo. — Then please do a dark brown.

explanations.title: Cultural notes: 방, 이발소 and 미용실
explanations.body:
머리방, whose literal meaning is “hair room”, is a popular term for 미용실 or 미장원 (a hair salon). Since the late 1990s many small businesses have dropped 실 (室), 원 (院) or 점 (店) and used the pure Korean 방 as part of their business names. Some of the popular 방’s in Korea are 노래방 (a karaoke bar), 빨래방 (a laundromat), 게임방, PC방, 꾸밈방 (a home interior shop) and 책방 (a bookstore).

이발소 or 이용원 (a barbershop) is a place where men get a haircut and a shave, and 미용실, 미장원 or 머리방 (a beauty parlor or hair salon) is its counterpart for women. However, it is also common for a man to get a haircut at 미용실.

lessons.title: 119. Ch 7 · Grammar A: the negating adverbs 안 and 못
lessons.subtitle: 안 먹어요 · 못 먹어요 · 공부 안 해요 · 잘 못 해요

explanations.title: Negating with 안 and 못
explanations.body: In English we use “not” to negate a verb, as in “He is not learning Japanese.” In Korean we negate a verb by placing 안 or 못 in front of it. 안 is translated as “not” and 못 as “cannot” or “unable to”.

examples.translation: gim seonsaengnimeun gimchireul an meogeoyo. — Mr. Kim does not eat kimchi. (He chooses not to.)
gim seonsaengnimeun gimchireul mon meogeoyo. — Mr. Kim cannot eat kimchi. (He is unable to.)

explanations.title: The difference
explanations.body: The first sentence (안) implies that Mr. Kim chooses not to eat kimchi (although he could eat it), and the second (못) means that he is unable to eat kimchi. 안 can negate action verbs as well as stative verbs, but 못 usually negates only action verbs.

rows: 가다 → 안 가다; 넓다 → 안 넓다
place 못 before an action verb
가다 → 못 가다; 마시다 → 못 마시다

explanations.title: Note 1: verbs made of a noun + 하다
explanations.body: To negate a verb constructed from “noun + 하다”, such as 공부하다 or 청소하다, place 안/못 between the noun and 하다. The book marks the wrong order with an asterisk: *저는 주말에 안 청소합니다 and *저는 주말에 못 청소합니다 are ungrammatical.

examples.translation: jeoneun jumare cheongso an hamnida. — I do not clean my house on the weekend.
jeoneun jumare cheongso mo tamnida. — I cannot clean my house on the weekend.

explanations.title: Note 2: when there is an adverb
explanations.body: When there is an adverb in a sentence, 안 and 못 negate the adverb, not the verb.

examples.translation: jeoneun suyeongeul jal mo tamnida. — I do not swim well. (I swim, but not well.)
jeoneun suyeongeul ppalli mo tamnida. — I do not swim quickly. (I swim, but not quickly.)

lessons.title: 120. Ch 7 · Grammar B: giving reasons with -아서/어서 (and thus; because)
lessons.subtitle: 비가 와서 · 작아서 · 맛있어서 · 안 먹어서 · 생일이어서

explanations.title: -아서/어서 for cause and effect
explanations.body: The conjunctive ending -아서/어서 can be interpreted as (1) “and then” (sequential events) and (2) “and thus” (cause and effect). The first meaning was covered in Chapter 5; here you meet the second. “It is raining and thus I can’t go hiking” is virtually the same as “Because it is raining, I can’t go hiking” or “Since it is raining, I can’t go hiking.” So -아서/어서 can be translated as “and therefore”, “so”, “because” or “since”. The first clause (비가 와서, it is raining, and thus …) is the cause and the second clause (등산 못 가요, I can’t go hiking) is the effect.

The last syllable contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
한식이 맛있다 → 한식이 맛있어서; 아침을 안 먹다 → 아침을 안 먹어서

lessons.title: 121. Ch 7 · Grammar C: asking for a service with -아/어 주세요
lessons.subtitle: 열어 주세요 · 닫아 주세요 · 가르쳐 주세요 · 도와 주세요 · 해 주세요

explanations.title: The auxiliary verb for providing service
explanations.body: Earlier you learned that the verbs 주다 and 드리다 (the honorific of 주다) mean “to give”. However, when 주다 or 드리다 is used as part of the auxiliary verb -아/어 주다 or -아/어 드리다, it implies that the subject provides or offers a service, or does something for someone else’s benefit. 친구가 책을 읽어 줍니다/드립니다 implies that my friend is (providing the service of) reading a book to someone else. So if you want someone to do something for you, ask with -아/어 주세요. Stative verbs do not work with -아/어 주다 and -아/어 드리다.

rows: The last syllable of an action verb stem contains ㅏ or ㅗ

The last syllable contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
문을 열다 → 문을 열어 주다 / 열어 드리다

explanations.title: -(으)ㄹ까요?
explanations.body: -(으)ㄹ까요? can be used when making an invitation or suggestion, when asking for thoughts or input, and when offering a service or favor. The subject of the sentence can be omitted when using -(으)ㄹ까요?.

A verb stem ends in a vowel

explanations.title: Three uses
explanations.body: 1. Making an invitation or suggestion. 2. Asking for thoughts or offering a favor. In a situation where the speaker offers a favor or service to the listener, we often combine -아/어 주다/드리다 with the expression, as in -아/어 줄까요 / 드릴까요? (The English is the book’s except for the rows I added.)

explanations.title: Activity 2: a question and an answer on a Korean-American website
explanations.body: Jungmin wants to get her hair done this weekend. On the “Koreans in America” website she finds this question and answer. The book glosses 추천하다 as “to recommend”. The English is mine; the book’s three comprehension questions have my answers below the text.

rows: Park Minchul Hair (박민철 헤어), in San Jose.
Why is that salon a good choice?
The hairdressers do hair well, so you will like it (and it is usually busy).
What is Jungmin advised to do before going, and why?
Make a reservation, because there are usually many people.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with so they can offer other activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: list and discuss businesses around town; order food and drink at a restaurant; ask for services at a hair salon or barber shop.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the negating adverbs 안 and 못; the conjunctive ending -아/어서 for cause and effect (and thus; because); the auxiliary verb -아/어 주다 used to express “the sense of providing service”; and the Sino-Korean syllables 소 (所), 음 (飮) and 점 (店).

lessons.title: 125. Ch 8 · Topic A: Traveling last weekend
lessons.subtitle: 지난 주말에 샌프란시스코에 갔습니다 · 출발 · 도착 · 돌아다니다 · 품 (品) · 복 (服)

explanations.title: What Chapter 8 teaches (지난 주말)
explanations.body:
Chapter 8, “Last Weekend”, has three topic presentations, four grammar points, activities, a self-evaluation and the core vocabulary.

When you finish the chapter you will be able to: comprehend and respond to simple information regarding weekend activities; narrate past weekend activities in a simple paragraph; and recognize and respond to different military ranks.

You will become familiar with: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the past tense “marker” -았/었; the auxiliary verb -아/어야 하다 or -아/어야 되다 (must; have to); the markers ~은/는, 만 and 도; the auxiliary verb -아/어 보다 (try; try -ing); and the Sino-Korean syllables 대 (大), 복 (服), 소 (小), 소 (少), 중 (中) and 품 (品).

explanations.title: Strategy: compound verbs that end in -가다, -오다 or -다니다
explanations.body: Previewing the Core Vocabulary you may have met verbs that end in -가다, -오다 or -다니다 (to go to and from; to attend), such as 돌아가다, 돌아오다 and 돌아다니다. They are compound verbs, made from two verbs: for example 돌아오다 consists of 돌다 and 오다. The stem of the first verb is followed by 아/어, which works as “glue”, and then comes the second verb. Koreans almost always express movement with -가다, -오다 or -다니다. To say “walk to school” they say 학교에 걸어가다 (“walk and go to school”) or 학교에 걸어오다 (“walk and come to school”); for “come in” they say 들어오다 (“be in and come”); for “return home” 집에 돌아가다 (“turn and go home”) or 집에 돌아오다 (“turn and come home”).

explanations.title: Officer ranks (장교 계급)
explanations.body: The book shows the officer ranks with their insignia (the insignia are pictures and are not reproduced). The Korean names and their English equivalents are from the book’s chart. 준위 is a warrant officer; in the chart there is no rank next to 준위 in the middle column (N/A).

explanations.title: The ladder
explanations.body: From the lowest of these ranks to the highest (the order follows the book’s chart and its example sentences: 준위 is just below 소위; 소령 is just above 대위; 중령 is just below 대령; 소장 is just above 준장; 중장 is just above 소장). The same three-way pattern 소 · 중 · 대 (young, middle, big) repeats in each group: 소위, 중위, 대위; 소령, 중령, 대령; and 소장, 중장, 대장, with 준장 (“deputy commander”) below 소장.

explanations.title: Sino-Korean in use: 大, 中, 小 and 少
explanations.body: Three of these four Chinese characters are used in ranks for officers. 大 (대), which means great, big or large, is used in 대위, 대령 and 대장. 中 (중), which means middle or medium, is used in 중위, 중령 and 중장. 小 (소), which means small or little, is used in 소형, “small style”. 少 (소), which means young or a few, is used in 소년 (young boy) and 소녀 (young girl). Which one is used for 소위, 소령 and 소장, 小 or 少? The book’s hint: which sounds better, “small officer” or “young officer”? (The answer, in the Core Vocabulary, is 少: “young officer”.)

lessons.title: 127. Ch 8 · Grammar A: the past tense marker -았/었
lessons.subtitle: 먹었습니다 · 갔어요 · 했어 · 봤어요 · 마셨어요 · 썼어요

explanations.title: Making the past tense
explanations.body: Recall the three speech styles indicated by verb endings attached to the stem of a verb: (1) formal polite -ㅂ니다/습니다, as in 먹습니다; (2) informal polite -아요/어요, as in 먹어요; and (3) informal blunt -아/어, as in 먹어. We use the three forms for the present tense: 나는 매일 김치를 먹습니다/먹어요/먹어 (“I eat kimchi every day”). To make the past tense of a verb, simply add the past tense “marker” 았/었 to the verb stem and then end it with the appropriate verb ending. The past tense “marker” is also known as the past tense suffix or infix.

rows: The last syllable of the verb stem contains ㅏ or ㅗ
add 았 and one of the endings (습니다/어요/어)
많다: 많 + 았 + 습니다 → 많았습니다; 많았어요; 많았어
The last syllable contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
add 었 and one of the endings
먹다: 먹 + 었 + 습니다 → 먹었습니다; 먹었어요; 먹었어
tables.title: verb stem + 았/었 + speech-style ending (습니다/어요/어)

examples.translation: naneun maeil gimchireul meokseumnida. — I eat kimchi every day.
eoje hanguksikdangeseo jeomsimeul meogeotseumnida. — Yesterday, I had lunch at a Korean restaurant.
baekwajeome sarami manatseumnida. — There were a lot of people in the department store.
doseogwaneseo chaegeul ilgeotseumnida. — I read a book in the library.

explanations.title: The conjugation rules are the same as for -아요/어요
explanations.body: Because the past tense marker 았/었 consists of 아/어 and ㅆ, it follows the same conjugation rules as the informal -아요/어요. When 았/었 is attached to a stem that ends in a vowel, the same deletion or contraction applies (see Chapter 2). The book’s table, with my forms:

rows: ㅏ → 았: last syllable 많 has ㅏ
ㅓ → 었: last syllable 먹 has ㅓ
deletion: 가 + 았 → 갔 (the same vowel is dropped)
ㅡ is dropped and 었 added: 쓰 → ㅆ + 었 → 썼
하 + 았 → 했: the only ㅏ-ending verb that behaves this way

explanations.title: Forms of more verbs
explanations.body: The forms below are mine; ㅂ irregular verbs behave as in Chapter 6 (즐겁다 → 즐거웠다). 이다 becomes 이었다 after a consonant and 였다 after a vowel.

lessons.title: 128. Ch 8 · Grammar B: trying and experience with -아/어 보다
lessons.subtitle: 먹어 봤어요 · 가 봤어요 · 살아 봤어요 · 먹어 보세요

explanations.title: Try; try -ing
explanations.body: In English, to express experimentation or experience we use the verb “try” or “try -ing”, as in “I tried kimchi for the first time” or “I tried opening the door.” In Korean we use the auxiliary verb -아/어 보다. This auxiliary verb is used with action verbs only.

rows: The last syllable of the stem contains ㅏ or ㅗ
살다 → 살아 보다; 가다 → 가아 보다 → 가 보다
The last syllable contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
먹다 → 먹어 보다; 읽다 → 읽어 보다
tables.title: action verb stem + 아/어 보다

examples.translation: gimchireul meogeo bwatseumnida. — I tried (eating) kimchi.
gimchi han beon meogeo boseyo. — Please try (eating) kimchi once.

explanations.title: Forms
explanations.body: The forms below are mine: the past form 봤어요 asks or says whether you have tried it; the request 보세요 asks someone to try it.

explanations.body: In the book partners take turns asking each other questions with -아/어 봤어요 from List A or List B; if the answer is negative, the asker suggests what to try with -아/어 보세요. explanations.title: Activity 1: how Koreans spend holidays and weekends
explanations.body: The book prints a short article and asks you to identify the activities and places in English. The article: 한국 사람들은 주말과 휴일에 TV나 영화를 많이 봅니다. 최근 한 조사에서는 TV나 영화 보기가 35%, 인터넷•컴퓨터가 28%, 운동 25%, 여행은 12%이었습니다. 여행 장소는 산 38%, 바닷가 25%, 호수•강 22%, 박물관 15%로 나타났습니다. The book glosses 조사 as “research; poll” and 장소 as “a place; site”. My reading of the figures:

examples.text: 한국 사람들은 주말과 휴일에 티브이나 영화를 많이 봅니다.
examples.translation: hanguk saramdeureun jumalgwa hyuire tibeuina yeonghwareul mani bomnida. — Koreans watch a lot of TV or movies on weekends and holidays.

explanations.title: Activity 1 (second set): General Ann Dunwoody and her family
explanations.body: The text is about General Ann Dunwoody, America’s first female four-star general, and her family. The book asks you to circle the rank words and the past-tense verbs and to name four facts about her family. The book glosses 되다 “to become”, 조종사 “a pilot” and 태어나다 “to be born”. The English is mine; the book’s first sentence reads 앤 던우디는 장군은, which is a typo for 앤 던우디 장군은; the date is spelled out.

rows: the third female Army helicopter pilot

examples.text: 앤 던우디 장군은 이천팔년 십일월 십사일에 대장으로 진급했습니다.
examples.translation: aen deonudi jangguneun icheonpallyeon sibirwol sipsaire daejangeuro jingeupaetseumnida. — General Ann Dunwoody was promoted to four-star general on November 14, 2008.
aenui gajogeun modu guninimnida. — Ann’s family are all soldiers.

examples.text: 앤의 할아버지 헨리 던우디는 육군 준장이었습니다.
examples.translation: aenui harabeoji helli deonudineun yukgun junjangieotseumnida. — Ann’s grandfather Henry Dunwoody was an Army brigadier general.
geurigo aenui abeojido yukgun junjangieotseumnida. — And Ann’s father was also an Army brigadier general.

examples.text: 앤의 언니는 세번째 육군 여자 헬리콥터 조종사가 되었습니다.

geurigo aenui nampyeoneun gonggun daeryeongieotseumnida. — And Ann’s husband was an Air Force colonel.

explanations.title: Activity 3: an alibi e-mail from PFC Ha Inyoung
explanations.body: At a military base in Seoul two laptop computers were stolen last Saturday; all servicemen in the barracks must report where they were from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. KATUSA soldier PFC Ha Inyoung sends this e-mail to his mother (the book’s header is 어머님, 안녕하세요? …; the e-mail addresses and the date line are left out, and the book glosses 오늘 as “today”). The English is mine.

rows: left the barracks for the supermarket
met ten friends from the barracks
had a bulgogi barbecue party and lunch

explanations.title: Dialog: my younger brother came to Monterey
explanations.body: Two Korean friends going to college in Monterey are talking about their last long weekend. They are friends, so they use the informal blunt style. (The English is mine; the book glosses 잘 지냈어 nowhere: 잘 지내다 is “to get along well”.)

lessons.title: 131. Ch 8 · Grammar C: the markers ~은/는, 만 and 도
lessons.subtitle: 오후에는 · 오후에만 · 오후에도 · 제 친구는 · 제 친구만 · 제 친구도

explanations.title: Three more markers
explanations.body: So far you have learned markers attached to nouns to show their grammatical function: the time marker 에, the subject marker 이/가, the location marker 에서, the object marker 을/를, the source marker 에서 and the direction marker (으)로. You now learn three more, including the topic marker ~은/는 that you met in Chapter 1. They differ from the earlier markers in that they can be attached not only to nouns but also to phrases (any of the underlined words and phrases of a sentence).

rows: as for; speaking of; when it comes to

explanations.title: Attaching them to different parts of a sentence
explanations.body: Adding the markers to the phrase 오후에 (in the afternoon) of 오후에 제 친구가 도서관에서 한국어를 공부합니다 (“My friend studies Korean in the library in the afternoon”) gives the first three sentences below. When the markers are attached to the subject or the object, the subject marker and the object marker are dropped. (The English is the book’s.)

examples.text: 오후에는 제 친구가 도서관에서 한국어를 공부합니다.
examples.translation: ohueneun je chinguga doseogwaneseo hangugeoreul gongbuhamnida. — As for in the afternoon, my friend studies Korean in the library.

examples.text: 오후에만 제 친구가 도서관에서 한국어를 공부합니다.
examples.translation: ohueman je chinguga doseogwaneseo hangugeoreul gongbuhamnida. — My friend studies Korean in the library only in the afternoon.

examples.text: 오후에도 제 친구가 도서관에서 한국어를 공부합니다.
examples.translation: ohuedo je chinguga doseogwaneseo hangugeoreul gongbuhamnida. — My friend studies Korean in the library in the afternoon as well.
je chinguga hangugeoreul gongbuhamnida. — My friend studies Korean.
je chinguman hangugeoreul gongbuhamnida. — Only my friend studies Korean.
je chingudo hangugeoreul gongbuhamnida. — My friend, as well, studies Korean.
je chinguneun hangugeoreul gongbuhamnida. — As for my friend, he studies Korean.
je chinguga hangugeoman gongbuhamnida. — My friend studies Korean only.
je chinguga hangugeodo gongbuhamnida. — My friend studies Korean as well.
je chinguga hangugeoneun gongbuhamnida. — As for Korean, my friend studies it.

explanations.title: The two functions of the topic marker
explanations.body:
The topic marker has two major functions: to indicate the topic and provide emphasis, and to provide contrast.

1. Topic and emphasis: the emphasized phrase generally moves to the front of the sentence, and the topic marker is usually translated as “as for”, “speaking of” or “when it comes to”.

2. Contrast: the topic marker puts the noun or phrase in contrast with other nouns or phrases.

examples.translation: hangugeoneun je chinguga gongbuhamnida. — As for Korean, my friend studies it. (The emphasized phrase moves to the front.)
doseogwaneseo gongbuhamnida. — I study in the library.
doseogwaneseoneun gongbuhamnida. — I study in the library (but not in other places).
ohue gongbuhamnida. — I study in the afternoon.
ohueneun gongbuhamnida. — I study in the afternoon (but not at other times).
je chinguga gongbuhamnida. — My friend studies.
je chinguneun gongbuhamnida. — My friend (but not other people) studies.

explanations.title: Follow-up 1 and 2: changing the marker (models)
explanations.body: In the book one partner reads a sentence from a card and the other adds or changes the marker to 만 or 도. The models (the English is mine):

rows: I read a book. → I read only books. (책도 읽습니다: I read books too.)
I eat hamburgers. → I eat pizza too.
I do not eat hamburgers. → I eat only pizza.

explanations.title: The forms
explanations.body: The forms below are mine: ~은/는 is 은 after a consonant and 는 after a vowel; 만 and 도 have one form.

lessons.title: 132. Ch 8 · Grammar D: obligation and urgency with -아/어야 하다/되다
lessons.subtitle: 해야 해요 · 해야 돼요 · 일어나야 해요 · 가야 했어요

explanations.title: Must; have to; should
explanations.body: In English we often use modals like “must”, “have (got) to” and “should” to express different degrees of obligation or urgency, as in “I must report it by six”, “You have to finish it” or “You should go with me.” When Koreans express obligation or urgency, they often use the auxiliary verb -아/어야 하다 or -아/어야 되다. Depending on the context it can be interpreted as “must”, “have to” or “should”.

rows: The final syllable of the verb stem contains ㅏ or ㅗ
닫다 → 닫아야 하다/되다; 오다 → 와야 하다/되다
The final syllable contains a vowel other than ㅏ or ㅗ
먹다 → 먹어야 하다/되다; 다니다 → 다녀야 하다/되다
tables.title: verb stem + 아/어야 하다 or 아/어야 되다

examples.translation: ohueneun sukjereul haeya dwaeyo. — I have to do my homework in the afternoon.

explanations.title: In the past and with the markers
explanations.body: Past tense: 해야 했어요 / 해야 됐어요 (“had to”). The markers of the previous lesson can be attached: 지난 주말에는 … (as for last weekend), 지난 주말에도 … (last weekend, too) and 지난 주말에만 … (only last weekend). The English is mine except for the first three examples above.

explanations.title: Activity 2: a short biography of John Steinbeck
explanations.body: The passage gives brief biographical data about John Steinbeck, the famous writer who was born in Salinas. The book asks you to circle the past-tense verbs and to write in English what happened to him in each year. The text is the book’s (the English and the table are mine). In the book’s passage the sentence about his books names two works in English: “1939년에 The Grapes of Wrath, 1962년에는 The Winter of Our Discontent를 썼습니다”, which is left out of the examples below because the titles are in English; the other sentences are given with the years spelled out.

rows: wrote The Grapes of Wrath; received the Pulitzer Prize
wrote The Winter of Our Discontent; received the Nobel Prize

explanations.title: How to use this list
explanations.body: The book’s Core Vocabulary lists the core words of the chapter with an example sentence for each (the sentences are the book’s; the book gives no English for them). Pairs written together in the book (도착(하다), 운전(하다), 출발(하다), 진급(하다), 축하(하다), 파티(하다), 집안일(하다), 시험(보다), 춤(~ 추다)) are on separate rows, and the grammar endings are written without the leading hyphen: 아/어 보다, 아/어야 하다, 아/어야 되다, 았/었. The example sentences with digits or Latin letters are respelled in Hangul (LA → 엘에이, UPS → 유피에스, 14일 → 십사 일, 4일 → 사 일, 19살 → 열아홉 살); 파티(하다) uses the book’s sentence for both rows, and the sentence of 거기 is the book’s.

explanations.title: Self-evaluation
explanations.body:
Recall the objectives of the chapter and ask yourself whether you have achieved them (the book asks you to tick Yes or No). If you tick “No” for any item, the book suggests: review that section on your own; find a study partner and review it as a pair or group; and tell your academic advisor or team leader which areas you need more help with so they can offer other activities tailored to your learning style and needs.

Now I am able to: comprehend and respond to simple information regarding weekend activities; narrate past weekend activities in a simple paragraph; recognize and respond to different military ranks.

Now I have a clear understanding of: the new words and phrases in the Core Vocabulary; the past tense “marker” -았/었; the auxiliary verb -아/어야 하다 or -아/어야 되다 (must; have to); the markers ~은/는, 만 and 도; the auxiliary verb -아/어 보다 (try; try -ing); and the Sino-Korean syllables 대 (大), 복 (服), 소 (小), 소 (少), 중 (中) and 품 (品).
